maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND
speechtext:
I have the honour of welcoming to this house the President of Ireland, Mr. Eamon de Valera.
Mr. de Valera is President of a state which is more than a country; it is the motherland of millions of citizens of many other lands. The emerald isle and its friendly, warm and hospitable people have endeared themselves to millions who have not the privilege of having Irish blood in their veins. Ireland is a land which has sent to the world poets and presidents and policemen. It is a small island, but it has been responsible for great things including nearly two million Canadians of Irish birth or descent.
Our two countries have the closest and friendliest of relations. They have worked together at the United Nations and elsewhere, closely and harmoniously for peace, security and freedom in the world.
We welcome our guest to this parliament, not only as President but also as a man of great personal distinction, of passionate patriotism, of intellectual achievement and of great moral integrity. We hope that the president and the minister for external affairs, Mr. Aiken, who is with him, and other members of the party will have a happy visit to Canada. They are very, very welcome.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all of us will join with the Prime Minister in his words of welcome to the President of the Republic of Ireland. The Prime Minister, with that modesty that all of Irish origin have, did not point out directly that he is a distinguished descendant of ancestors among those two million Irish or of Irish origin who came to Canada and have established themselves here. Indeed, outside of the emerald isle, the United Kingdom, and the United States there are more persons of Irish origin in Canada than in any other country of the world. We welcome the President for what he is, the position he occupies, his contribution to world peace as president of the league of nations and as one
whose dedication has been to good relations with the other countries of the world.
I had the privilege of visiting the republic in 1961, when my wife and I were guests of the President and Mrs. de Valera for lunch. At that time I was able to view something of what Ireland's contribution had been to Canada. On that occasion I presented a plaque in commemoration of what had been done by Thomas D'Arcy McGee, who in 1848 left Ireland in rather precipitated circumstances and in 1864 or 1865 became one of the tribunes of our confederation. I would point out that only very recently have we discovered, as a result of the writing of the history of Canada by Gustave Lanctot, that the Irish were the first to find North America. Up to the present time it has been generally believed it was the Vikings or people from the Nordic countries, but according to this historian the Irish were here in 874 A.D., some 660 years before Jacques Cartier discovered Canada.
I recall with deep interest my visit to Ireland and an experience that I hope the house will allow me to clarify once and for all. Before I arrived there the Canadian ambassador received a cable to the effect that I would be arriving and Champagne would be with me. That caused a great deal of surprise and consternation. One of the members of my staff, Mr. Gilbert Champagne, was in my party, and it was only after arrival that the matter was clarified not only for the Canadian embassy but also for our hosts in Ireland.
I join in welcoming this distinguished visitor, and I hope that for many years to come he will continue to adorn the position he holds; that he will pursue the ways of peace and the leadership he has given to his own country, as well as through the United Nations in the interests of peace everywhere.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party join with the government and the official opposition in extending a welcome to the President of the Republic of Ireland. Mr. de Valera is one of the great figures of Irish history. He has dedicated his life to his belief in the right of the Irish people to govern themselves, and in his struggle to bring that belief to fruition he was the outstanding leader of the Irish rebellion and for the past quarter of a century has been the leader of the Irish people.

Distinguished. Visitor
One of the great characteristics of the President of Ireland has been his unyielding integrity. This has been paid tribute to not only by his friends but even by his opponents. Mr. Lloyd George once wrote of him "Mr. de Valera is perfectly unique, and this poor distracted world can be thankful that he was unique". Mr. Speaker, he has used his unique gifts not only for the benefit of his own people but for the benefit of mankind at large. He was, as has already been mentioned, president in 1932 of the league of nations council, and in 1938 president of the league of nations assembly. Today Irish forces are partners with Canadians in the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus.
As one who was bom in Scotland, we Scots have a deep feeling of kinship with the Irish since we both have had some trouble with the English in days gone by. However, our approach was different. The Irish chose to fight them; we infiltrated into England and took over all the positions of influence. The end results however, Mr. Speaker, I think will in the long run be for the good of humanity.
Today the President of Ireland is an honoured guest in Canada, he is full of honors and we bid him a thousand welcomes.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and with the leaders of the other parties in this house in welcoming President Eamon de Valera to our midst. We pray that his visit to Canada will convey to him the keen and warm friendship which all Canadians have toward his country and toward himself. As I look back on the period of history which Mr. de Valera represents I cannot help but think of him as a man who put aside his own personal interests and dedicated his life to a dream, saw that dream become a nation, and then had the privilege of leading that nation to a position of respect and high regard amongst all freedom loving peoples of the world. Thus on behalf of our party I join with others in saying welcome to Canada.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is also a pleasure for us, on this side of the house, to extend the warmest welcome to Canada to the President of the Republic of Ireland.
In the province of Quebec there are a great number of people of Irish origin, and we are very glad and very proud to have them as Canadian citizens and citizens of the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I think we can assure the President of the Republic of Ireland that the history of the people and the President of Ireland in the conquest of their country's independence is well known in the province of Quebec. The people of Ireland has certainly set an example for us and the whole world by its courage and energy. We are glad to welcome in our country the President of this valiant nation.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF IRELAND
speechtext: May I take this opportunity of extending to all honourable Senators and all hon. members of the house, especially those of Irish origin, an invitation to meet the President of Ireland in the Speaker's chamber shortly. We will meet there within a few minutes, and I hope we will have a quorum left in the house.

subtopic: FRASER VALLEY, B.C.-REPORTED DANGER DUE TO DELAYED RUN-OFF

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FRASER VALLEY, B.C.-REPORTED DANGER DUE TO DELAYED RUN-OFF
speechtext: wish to direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Current reports indicate an increased flood threat in the Fraser river area due to delayed run-off from the snowpack. Does the minister consider the situation as being a cause for concern and, if so, is he satisfied with the diking arrangements?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: FRASER VALLEY, B.C.-REPORTED DANGER DUE TO DELAYED RUN-OFF
speechtext:
I know the hon. member is referring to the fact that we have had an abnormally late, cold season in British Columbia with the result that at the week end the flow at Hope, which is our checkpoint, was running at the rate of
250.000	feet per second only. In the flood year of 1948, on May 28 it was running at
535.000 feet per second. In the case of a river having a catchment area as great as that of the Fraser, there is always concern when melt conditions extend so late in the year; and when all the forces of nature are turned against man it is difficult to make a prediction.
The ultimate solution lies, of course, in the report I laid on the table six weeks ago, the report of the Fraser river board. I got in touch with the responsible minister of the British Columbia government, Mr. Williston who replied at once and is now preparing the engineering study on the reinforcement of the dikes in the lower Fraser valley from Hope to the mouth at a cost of about $5 million. Then we will proceed under the Canada Water Conservation Act to make provision for the building of a number of small dams on the tributaries of the Fraser where the fish will not be interfered with.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: REPRESENTATION BY COUNSEL OF PERSONS DETAINED FOR DEPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. members for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) asked questions about Mr. Harry Hooper who was deported from Canada recently. Four main questions were asked.
First, was Mr. Hooper advised that he was entitled to counsel?
Second, was he given a chance to exercise that right?
Third, was he aware that he could get legal counsel free of charge?
Fourth, was he told that he would remain in prison until he had answered the questions?
Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of the matter and with the leave of the house, I would like to answer each one of these questions.
Mr. Hooper had already been deported from Canada three times. Every time he was informed of his right to legal counsel. The last time, on March 16, he fell under the jurisdiction of the immigration branch. The inquiry was postponed until March 23 and
Inquiries of the Ministry Mr. Hooper was told that he had another chance of seeking legal counsel if he wanted to be represented at the hearing by a lawyer.
At the opening of the inquiry, on March 23, he was again informed that, if he wished, he could be represented by counsel. He was also told that it did not have to be a lawyer, but that it could be a relative, a friend, a priest, a clergyman or any other person interested in his welfare. He was then asked whether he wanted to be represented and he replied he had nothing to say and the special investigator could do as he pleased.
When the inquiry was reopened, on April 7, Mr. Hooper was told once again he had the right to be represented by counsel and was asked if he had taken any steps to get one. He refused to answer. Mr. Hooper was clearly informed of his right to be represented by counsel.
With regard to exercising one's right to secure a lawyer, I think that point was raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and I must say first of all that persons who want to be represented by counsel, when their deportation case is heard, must do it at their own expense. That provision has been in the Immigration Act for several years. The immigration branch sees to it that the interested parties are aware of their right to get a lawyer. If they want to be represented by counsel, investigations are postponed to enable them to get a lawyer.
As I said before, Mr. Hooper, although knowing that he had the right to get help from a lawyer, never indicated that he wanted it. He could have tried to get free legal assistance from the jail's lawyer or from various benevolent societies which offer such services. He knew about these societies. The authorities of the Don jail have confirmed the fact that members of these societies regularly visit the jail and that prisoners are well acquainted with their services.
As for the duration or term of the detention, Mr. Hooper was advised that he would be detained until he was ready to answer questions. Refusal to answer questions is, under the Immigration Act, a violation liable to prosecution. Mr. Hooper answered that he did not care, that anyway he had nothing better to do.
Immediately after the adjournment of the inquiry on March 23 the special investigator submitted the matter to the headquarters of the department of immigration in Ottawa in order to obtain instructions. It has been decided to reopen the investigation and to proceed taking into account other evidence available.
I wish to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the available evidence was

Inquiries of the Ministry to Mr. Hooper's advantage and that it was in his interest that such supplementary evidence be examined.
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have answered the four main questions which hon. members asked last Friday. My answers may be summarized as follows:
First, Mr. Hooper had been informed of his right to obtain legal counsel.
Second, he had every opportunity to do so, had he so wished.
Third, he was aware that he could secure free legal advice.
Fourth, immediately after the inquest of March 23, while Mr. Hooper had been informed that he would be detained until he answered the questions, the matter was brought to the attention of the immigration department at Ottawa for instructions. Shortly after Mr. Hooper was specifically informed that refusal to answer the questions constituted under the Immigration Act, an offence which would entail legal proceedings.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION BY COUNSEL OF PERSONS DETAINED FOR DEPORTATION

Mr. Speaker, during all his period of detention, Mr. Hooper was held under the Immigration Act, the provisions of Which allow the detention of any individual who is in Canada without a visa, before carrying out a deportation order. On the other hand, as the deportation order has to be carried out as soon as possible, the department must make the necessary arrangements for the deportation.
This involves not only transportation arrangements but also arrangements with the country where the individual is to be deported, in order that all the papers be ready at the time this individual is transferred from Canada to another country.
During the period of detention, I think that legally, and under several other sections of the Immigration Act, the department had every right to bring the case before the court. I believe the department had full right to hold Mr. Hooper without making any charge, and this under sections of the act other than that allowing the department to detain an individual who holds no visa allowing him to remain legally in Canada.
As concerns the second question of the hon. member, I believe what happened-and, Mr. Speaker you mentioned it yourself- was the result of an error in translation: the part where I said Mr. Hooper had had every opportunity to obtain assistance from counsel was not translated, and when the leader of the New Democratic party asked why that had not been allowed, I said this question should be addressed to Mr. Hooper, as I thought the hon. member was aware of my reply.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration a supplementary or perhaps a related question. subtopic: REPRESENTATION BY COUNSEL OF PERSONS DETAINED FOR DEPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Oxford repeated a question he had asked on April 17 regarding Stylianos Yiannopolous, a Greek seaman who


deserted his ship in Canada. The hon. member will recall that some weeks ago my executive assistant provided him with an oral report on the Yiannopolous case and he agreed that a reply in the house was unnecessary. However, in view of this last question I am pleased to provide the following information.
This man deserted his ship in June 1961. He was apprehended in London, Ontario on January 16, 1964. A deportation inquiry was ordered on January 23 but was deferred at Mr. Yiannopolous' request in order to give him time to obtain counsel. He did get a lawyer who asked for a further deferral. It will be seen, therefore, that contrary to the assertion of the hon. member for Oxford, Mr. Yiannopolous did get counsel and was represented throughout all proceedings against him.
The inquiry on the deportation order was held on February 4. Mr. Yiannopolous appealed, and his appeal was heard and dismissed by the immigration appeal board on February 20. Representations on his behalf were then made to me. I reviewed these carefully but decided on March 24 to proceed with the deportation order. Until this time all the delays arose in order to give Mr. Yiannopolous time to get counsel and to appeal the decision.
After the appeal was dismissed the department decided to prosecute him under the Immigration Act in accordance with departmental policy aimed at curbing the serious incidence of ship desertion in Canada. The charge was laid on April 14 and was dismissed on the ground, I believe, that the man's name was improperly spelled, notwithstanding the fact that he pleaded guilty to the charge. He was deported from Canada on April 28. The procedures in this case were entirely legal, but I agree that the period of detention after the appeal was dismissed was too lengthy. Arrangements have been made to avoid such delays in future.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before the committee rose last Thursday evening to report progress on this resolution, I was dealing with the high average cost of acquiring and clearing blighted property in our large cities. I mentioned that the average cost in the two major cities of Montreal and Toronto was approximately $300,000 per acre. I should have pointed out perhaps that these costs are partly offset by recoveries from re-use, but Canadian experience has shown that the loss of about one third of the gross expenditures on the most comprehensive redevelopment projects must be borne and is being borne by the governments concerned.
As indicated by this resolution, the federal government in the national interest is prepared to absorb in future a substantial portion of these losses. Redevelopment, however, will remain essential for those cities in Canada which have depreciated beyond the point of no return, and this need is likely to continue for some time if corrective action is not taken.
It must be borne in mind, however, that redevelopment involves not only high costs

National Housing Act
but considerable disruption as well. As a result of redevelopment moves, families are uprooted and often move away from their neighbours and from the areas with which they are familiar. In this connection it must be borne in mind also that although housing conditions may be improved as a result of redevelopment some families will move away and will move into areas that are similarly overcrowded and inadequate. All levels of government, therefore, must be continually conscious of the fact that something must be done in this direction. The economic and social characteristics of redevelopment should spur us all in the search for devices and techniques which will prevent the deterioration of areas to the point where clearance and the bulldozer offer the only remedy.
Our cities need the means to face up to blight with a proper and more comprehensive set of techniques than merely clearance. The problem is too complex to be dealt with simply by a bulldozer. What is needed is a municipal program which in the early stages would stop the spread of structural and environmental decay and could generate the physical, economic and, more important, the social renewal of declining areas or areas about to decline. Such an urban renewal program would encompass, therefore, three activities, not only the clearance type of redevelopment with which I have dealt but also rehabilitation and conservation. Urban blight usually casts its shadow before it and I firmly believe that it can be turned back, if the warning signs are heeded, but the situation must be attended to when these warning signs first become noticeable. Surely some rehabilitative action can be taken before the point of no return, that is, before bulldozing becomes the only solution.
There are large areas in some of our cities which are beginning to show signs of blight. Frequently they are the older sections, sections where there is increased traffic flow from trucks and other slow moving, heavy vehicles, and sections which have been infiltrated with non-residential use. I believe that the spread of blight in many of these residential neighbourhoods can be corrected if vigorous action is taken soon enough. Indeed, we have only to go into some of the older cities in Canada-I am thinking of Halifax, Toronto, Montreal and Hamilton, though more particularly of the first three mentioned-to see, if they cannot be restored and if we cannot preserve the good qualities of some of these old residential sections. I am sure that the splendid residential qualities of some of these older neighbourhoods can be restored by a combination of public and private action.

Some of the more badly decayed buildings may well have to be demolished, and uses of land, which depreciated the environment may have to be terminated. Undoubtedly new facilities, new utilities and new services will have to be installed and, above all, the owners of private property can and should be encouraged and helped to maintain and improve their properties to reasonable standards. This can only be done, however, by a combination of public and private action.
The government is convinced that rehabil-tation of older neighbourhoods must form an important component of any comprehensive urban renewal program, and paragraphs (a), (b), and (c), of the resolution indicate that the government has this in mind.
The third activity which I have mentioned is conservation, which means action to prevent the decay of healthy residential sections that now exist. This in effect is the first and most important-perhaps I should say the most effective-weapon in the prevention of urban decay and, while it is a necessary component of a total program of urban renewal, it is one which by its very nature requires the adoption and enforcement of zoning and maintenance bylaws by the cities, and it falls largely within the purview of provincial and local governments.
This then is the comprehensive program of renewal which I see as the means of helping municipalities to overcome the spread of urban blight. As I have already mentioned, the program involves the redevelopment areas which have depreciated beyond repair, the rehabilitation of areas which can be given extended useful life by positive action, if taken soon enough, and the conservation of all that which is good in the existing urban fabric.
The bill to be presented when the resolution is adopted offers three things to give broader scope and to encourage new kinds of programs of urban renewal in Canada's cities. First, there are additional incentives for redevelopment projects; second-and this is in paragraph (a)-federal aid in the form of contributions or loans for municipal rehabilitation in urban renewal areas and, third N.H.A. loans on existing houses in urban renewal areas will be possible under the new legislation.
In the existing redevelopment provisions, that is, in the act as it now stands, there is the requirement that there must be a substantial residential content in the area, either before or after redevelopment. It is, I think, apparent that comprehensive urban renewal cannot be limited to residential property. The development of fine cities in Canada requires that municipalities be able to clear areas of

blight and slums, whatever their present use may be, whether it is commercial, industrial or residential.
The cost of acquiring and clearing blighted areas is presently shared fifty-fifty by the federal and municipal governments, although in some provinces the provincial government bears part of the municipal share. The municipal share of capital cost is relatively high and undoubtedly this has restricted action, that is, corrective action, in the past. It is the government's intention to widen the act to help municipalities finance their share of capital costs through loans. Again I would refer to paragraph (a) of the resolution.
In addition, the application of federal urban redevelopment grants is to be extended from acquisition and clearance to cover the cost of preparing cleared land for disposal for the re-use proposed. In other words, funds might be provided for worn out municipal services, street and traffic improvements in the selected areas, and for sidewalks and off-street parking in the approved urban renewal areas.
So much for the changes in respect to redevelopment. What of rehabilitation? In this area the federal government now offers aid to the provinces, or to the municipalities that the provinces may designate, to assist in the process of urban rehabilitation. It is now proposed that the federal government offer grants and loans for municipal works in designated areas, where these works are necessary to arrest the spread of blight and contribute to renewal, provided of course the specific area is part of a comprehensive renewal scheme.
Successful rehabilitation depends, however, not just on public works but on private improvements as well, and I believe that the provisions contemplated by this measure will supplement what the private sector of the economy is expected to do. To facilitate private improvements and the fluidity of property markets in renewal areas, the N.H.A. insured loan provisions will be extended to existing housing in designated areas. Furthermore, as the resolution indicates, if private lenders are reluctant to lend in these areas, C.M.H.C. loans will be made available.
As indicated by the resolution, the proposed legislation contains a number of other items, in addition to the urban renewal and public housing provisions to which I alluded briefly last Thursday and again today. In this connection I would draw hon. members' attention to the provisions of paragraph (f) which authorize loans to co-operative and charitable institutions to assist in the construction of accommodation for university students and their families, and which authorize an increase of $100 million for this purpose.
National Housing Act
Paragraph (g) provides that loans to provinces will continue in connection with the construction and expansion of sewage facilities, with forgiveness of 25 per cent of those loans, and paragraph (h) provides an additional $500 million for all purposes, which is to be a charge on the consolidated revenue fund.
Paragraph (h) provides for an increase in the fund to take care of the objectives I have been dealing with during the last few minutes and on Thursday evening, an increase from $2 billion to $2J billion.
Paragraph (i) provides for a special fund of an additional $100 million for secondary mortgages.
Paragraph (j) is intended to increase the loan ratio for insured loans. Hon. members who have read the legislation or who were present will recall that in the last session this was taken care of for a limited period by another method. The loan ratio will be increased under the proposed legislation and there are administrative changes which are contemplated.
At the beginning of my remarks I mentioned there would be an opportunity following the resolution stage to consider the proposed bill in all its detail. I wanted to use this occasion, however, to speak generally about the broad purposes of the measure and the objectives which prompted the government to put forward the important changes about which I have been speaking.
In bringing these remarks to a conclusion I should like to repeat the two most important aims to which I referred some days ago. First there is the wish, the hope, more than that, the intent of the government to do its part in improving standards of housing and housing conditions for those most in need and, in fact, for all Canadians in the elimination of the degrading housing conditions which exist in certain parts of this country, a challenging but realistic objective and one which the government believes should be accorded a high priority in federal housing policy. Second, we can no longer rest content with a federal urban renewal policy, which is confined to clearance and redevelopment alone. Such a policy by implication accepts the process of decay and rot as if it were something inevitable and natural. We know there is no automatic private market process which regenerates urban areas as they decline. Therefore, the government believes that if there is to be such a regenerative process it must be developed as a matter of public policy. We propose to encourage and help the provinces and their municipalities to develop it together with the federal government and its agencies.

National Housing Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
We do not wish to delay the passage of this resolution but in our opinion, or at least in my opinion, it is of such importance to the people of Canada that some attention should be paid to it. We welcome the resolution and look forward with a great deal of interest to scrutinizing carefully the legislation to implement it.
I should like to say to the minister that we particularly welcome his statement that this resolution represents a basic change in the concept and a completely fresh approach to the question of housing. We believe that a basic change and a fresh approach are urgently needed. In our opinion, housing is one of the most important parts of the responsibility of any modem government. Indeed, it ranks with matters such as medical care and old age pensions as among the most important questions facing Canadians at all levels of government. I am reminded of an excellent statement on housing and the part it plays in our lives-a statement which was made in an address to the Canadian housing design council by James A. Murray a well known architect, who had this to say of the purpose of housing:
It shelters the physiological functions of living, sleeping, eating, bathing. It shelters the care and education of children and the private and public domestic life of its occupants. It serves as haven to individuals hard pressed by the group obligations and pressures of modem life. It is a symbol and expression of its occupant in particular and its times in general.
We also welcome the emphasis which the minister has placed upon the need for public housing and the need for the redevelopment of decayed areas. Even more-and I speak particularly for my own constituents-we welcome the attention which has been paid for the first time to the need for the rehabilitation and renovation of the existing stock of housing in areas which are by no means slums, but which can easily become slums if no governmental responsibility is accepted. I agree with the remark the minister made when he said that by international standards most people in Canada are well housed. The emphasis, there, must be placed on the word "most".

In another address delivered to the Canadian housing design council by Mr. Ian Mac-lennan, executive director of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Mr. Mac-lennan makes the same statement as was made by the minister in the house. But Mr. Maclennan goes on at once to say:
Nevertheless, there are large numbers of low income families living in desperately inadequate dangerous, and sometimes tragic housing conditions. Thousands of Canadian families can't afford decent housing without some form of subsidy.
It is possible, in theory, to build so many new houses through the private market that adequate housing eventually becomes available even for the very poor. This is called the ''filtering down" process and it's never worked very well. It is an expensive and uncertain way of providing housing for low income families. Expensive because it requires sufficient new housing not only to meet their particular needs, but enough to improve the housing circumstances of everyone else as well. It's uncertain because it requires a public policy to sustain the demand for new housing far beyond the normal market requirements.
Then he goes on to say:
The most direct, economic and certain way of meeting the problem is to build, buy or lease a stock of housing and allocate it to the families who need it most, at prices they can afford to pay. By whatever method this housing is acquired, subsidies of one sort or another are needed, and this is usually called public housing.
Then the author goes on to refer to one of the greatest failures in our whole domestic housing policy in Canada, that is, the failure to meet the need for public housing. Admittedly, this country has done very well through the National Housing Act in financing the housing of the top 50 per cent of the people of Canada. A tremendous stock of houses has been built. But the endeavours at the different levels of government to meet the needs of those who have the greatest housing difficulties, the other 50 per cent, have been a failure. I welcome the frank words of the minister on this subject and the provision contained in the resolution. I hope the legislation will change the picture, because the picture certainly needs to be changed.
Mr. Maclennan goes on to say:
The National Housing Act provides for the construction and operation of public housing in Canada-on the initiation of municipalities, with the approval of the provinces. In 14 years the program has produced only 8,000 subsidized dwelling units-
That is somewhat different from the figure the minister gave us. I think he said that
9,000	were subsidized out of 12,000 units built. Mr. Maclennan's figure may be earlier; he says that in 14 years the program has produced only 8,000 subsidized dwelling units. He goes on to say:
-and there is no doubt that thousands more are needed. An approximate comparison indicates that in 1961 the British paid about $3.15 per capita

in annual subsidies for public housing, the Americans about $0.80 and the Canadians just under $0.10.
I referred earlier to a speech made by Mr. Murray on housing and architecture. I wish to read something he has to say on this subject.
In the 1950-60 period some 3,600 units of subsidized housing were laboriously achieved alongside some 1,263,000 private housing starts or 2/5 of 1 per cent of the private market. This should indicate that as a nation we are so rich we don't need it, so poor we can't afford it, or so ineffective we can't do it. It is not the purpose of this paper to assess which is nearer the truth.
Although Mr. Murray was too tactful to assess which is nearer the truth, we will assert that it is not because we are so rich that we do not need this public housing in Canada, and it is not because we are so poor that we cannot afford it. The real reason is that we have been so ineffective that we have not been able to do it; and I hope this resolution and the legislation which will follow will bring a change in that field. Mr. Murray goes on to say that we have made excellent progress in home building for the upper income brackets. He says:
This home builder segment of the total housing machine is extraordinarily effective and the private builder plus private client, plus government insured mortgage system is tremendously effective in the top income third and through the upper half of the middle third-all this is done under the agreeable twin euphemisms of private housing and home ownership.
If we are to take seriously the need for housing, which is so tremendously important to the families of Canadians, including not only those in the big cities but those in other communities as well, we have to accept the lead of other countries, acknowledge the need for public subsidized housing, and change the picture; and I welcome the indication the resolution gives, that the government intends to bring in legislation for this purpose. Because of the fact that in Canada the responsibility is divided, it seems to me the danger is that we do not have an adequate amount of planning and co-operation between the different levels of government. I fully appreciate that there is a constitutional problem involved in direct communication between the federal government, which is responsible for a substantial amount of the financing of housing, and the municipal governments which are, as has been said, the creatures of provincial legislatures. But the time has come when, if we mean what we say about co-operative federalism in a vital and urgent subject like housing, we need constant conference among those who represent great urban areas like Toronto-I mention that first because I happen to live there-or Montreal, Vancouver or Winnipeg,
National Housing Act
the representatives of municipalities, which have the local initiative to carry out these plans, the provinces which have their share of responsibility, and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
It is not good enough to pass legislation which enables the federal government to do certain things. There is a great and urgent necessity for strong leadership; and I welcome the statement of determination that I read in the minister's speech. It is to be found at page 3717 of Hansard, where he said, if my recollection is correct, that the goal of this legislation is frankly ambitious and it encompasses nothing less than a decent standard of living for all Canadians. That is a laudable objective, I say to the minister; but it cannot be accomplished without the most vigorous initiatives and the highest degree of co-operation among the different levels of government.
I want to refer for a moment to a part of the city of Toronto-I do so because I represent a riding in that city-where people have lived for 50 or 60 years in a very pleasant but not wealthy locality with good schools, excellent recreation centres and other things of this sort. But unless steps are taken, and taken soon, to put the impetus of government financing behind the rehabilitation, the renewal of that sort of area which is by no means a slum area or one suffering slum conditions, and unless the same energy is employed that is going into financing the building of suburban areas for the upper income groups, in the course of time we are going to find that we have failed in the laudable objective the minister has put forward.
What is needed in respect of the rehabilitation of some of these central areas of the city? What is a comprehensive scheme of urban renewal? Again, Mr. Chairman, I have reference to the speech made by Mr. Maclen-nan, because he puts it much better than I could, to the Canadian housing design council on April 22 of this year. This speech was given at the Royal Ontario museum, Toronto. Mr. Maclennan said this:
A comprehensive scheme of urban renewal would encompass a whole range of aids to reestablish confidence and vitality in deteriorating neighbourhoods. These would include, besides redevelopment and public housing at least four other measures.
(1)	Refurbishing of community services such as streets, lighting, parks and schools. This would depend on financial aid to the municipality for help in replacing utilities and facilities in parts of the area being developed. This is important because lending institutions are unlikely to invest in renewal areas which are in unsatisfactory condition.
(2)	Partial rehabilitation for houses which do not require total clearance. This must be done quickly if the deterioration of the buildings and their surroundings are not to reach a point where

National Housing Act
it will not be financially wise to invest in repairs. The basic demands of rehabilitation are to use what we have that is worth using, and to keep costly redevelopment to a minimum.
I commend that statement to the minister. Redevelopment schemes at the centre of big cities are apt to be very expensive; they do not meet the neighbourhood needs; the people are sometimes put out and expensive apartments are built in their place; commercial areas grow up-and this may be perfectly all right-or office buildings. This is perfectly good planning; but if it is rehabilitation of what we have already that is needed, this type of costly revelopment is a great disservice to the people of Canada. Third, he says:
Financial assistance in the form of loans to owners of existing houses (in areas included in the urban renewal program) to increase their marketability, or to assist those wishing to rehabilitate their own dwellings. Through this plan residential buildings could be given additional life of many years.
I understand the legislation that is proposed will enable this to be done, and I welcome that very warmly because I think it is an important change of direction. I only hope it is followed up with energy by whoever is responsible. I do not know whether this minister is to continue with the responsibility indefinitely, but if he is I say to him that this part of the program should be followed up with the greatest energy, because I think it is very important. Mr. Maclennan goes on to say:
Neighbourhood conservation through the enforcement of building maintenance codes and occupancy bylaws.
That is not a matter, of course, for the federal government. Then he says:
A combined attack of public and private enterprise on urban blight through such a comprehensive plan could alter the face of our cities in a substantial and dramatic manner,
I believe that is what we can get if this legislation is effectively put into operation, and to be put into operation it needs, as I say, co-operation between the various levels of government. I want to give an illustration of a lack of adequate co-operation, as it seems to me, in this field of housing in relation to a well meant effort that went astray. I happen to know something about it, and I asked a question about it in the house, by putting my question on the order paper. It was answered in Hansard of May 6, 1964. My question related to the cost of a partnership development project entered into between the province of Ontario and central mortgage and housing for the acquisition of farm lands in the township of Scarborough. This appears at page 2971 of Hansard and it concerned land in the neighbourhood of Malvern
[Mr. Brewin.l
which was intended to be acquired land for low cost housing. My question asked:
What was the total sum of money paid out to farmers who owned the lands expropriated for the purpose?
It turned out that it was something over $2,300,000. The farms were expropriated in 1953 and I asked what housing developments, if any, had taken place under the project. The answer was that the lands have not yet been developed. After the farms were expropriated some of the land acquired for this joint housing project was rented back to the farmers, but no action was taken in respect to this land assembly at all. The reason will become apparent later.
Then I asked what was the cost in interest of this acquisition, apart from paying off the farmers, the reply was that the cost in interest which had accrued to March 31, 1964 was $765,070, with legal survey and sundry charges of $77,411. The net recovery from the rental of land and buildings was $93,401.
Then I asked whether any of this land had been sold, but only small parcels had been sold to the board of education and to other bodies of that sort. Certain small parcels had been leased.
Finally I asked:
If no serious development has taken place or is contemplated in the near future, what do the government of Canada and the government of Ontario propose to do with the lands in question?
The answer was as follows:
It is intended to make this land available for urban development as soon as the necessary municipal trunk services reach the area. Plans for a comprehensive neighbourhood will be prepared at the appropriate time. Land will be set aside for community facilities and for public housing projects to accommodate families of low income.
This answer to my question indicates a serious lack of intelligent, over-all and cooperative planning. We are told why this land was acquired and what the cost in interest amounted to, and nothing has been done with it. The reason is that there had not been the necessary municipal trunk services to reach the area. The land is not serviced and there are no plans to service it.
I was very happy to see in this resolution the statement that, included in the new legislation would be a provision whereby it would be possible to authorize the corporation to make loans to provinces to assist in the construction or expansion of sewage treatment projects, and to authorize the corporation to forgive repayment of 25 per cent of the principal and interest on any loans made to provinces or to municipalities for this purpose in respect of work completed by March 31, 1967. If we are going to develop new low cost housing projects through government

partnerships-which is an admirable concept -the municipality concerned should be consulted at the beginning, and the necessary arrangements made to ensure that at some appropriate period services will be made available. Otherwise the government is putting farmers off their land and speculating whether or not at a later date they will take a substantial loss. This acquisition to which I referred was in 1953, 11 years ago, and the land has just been left as it is. True, it has been rented back to the farmers, but the housing project was never started and I think the reason was that which I mentioned, lack of adequate planning at the time.
Before I sit down I should like to call to the attention of the minister another matter which, while it is local in one sense, is I think duplicated in many other parts of Canada, certainly in urban areas and cities. The minister will recall that a deputation from the city of Toronto, including Alderman Mrs. Birchard, and the commissioner of planning, presented a brief on the problem of homeless men in the city of Toronto. This brief pointed out that in the city of Toronto there is a serious problem in accommodating homeless single men who are aging and without employment.
I am not going to go over the whole story. Many of these men are over 50, have had little schooling and have few skills. The brief points out the lack of facilities to fill in the spare time of these persons. As the minister will recall, the brief speaks of a good neighbours club which was started in 1957 in a converted house provided by the city. The initial membership of 300 has now grown to over 1,900. I would urge, as the brief also urged, that the amendments to the National Housing Act should deal with the plight of these men who are so placed because of social and economic changes beyond their control. I submit it would be appropriate and desirable to include amendments to the National Housing Act so that it would be possible not only to provide such men with adequate living accommodation but also to make available centres where, whether living in housing projects or not, they could find daytime shelter and occupation, recreation and job training. This is the request of the municipalities. I hope the minister will be able to give a favourable response to it, because these are people who are in urgent need, not only in the city from which I happen to come but in many other cities throughout Canada. National Housing Act
-the person in charge of the corporation's Montreal office also died a few days ago of a heart attack.

Will the municipalities be in a position to undertake municipal works programs?
Do we have at the present time that committee which, I believe, is required to communicate with the municipal and provincial authorities and the federal government, and allow us to adopt policies agreeable to each of the concerned groups, so that we could rest assured that as soon as the act is passed, it can be immediately enforced. Unfortunately we in Quebec have had, in the past, some rather difficult experience with federal legislation. I do not bear any grudge against anyone, but I know that on account of our very special context in Quebec, certain federal measures have always been difficult to administer.
I would like to refer more particularly to the fact that we have in Quebec a legislation providing for a 3 per cent rebate on the interest paid on a loan directly granted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or by another organization vouched for by the corporation. The 3 per cent interest is connected with the assessment of the house itself. This assessment comes under the jurisdiction of the investigators of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It happens sometimes-I know personal and typical

examples-that assessors under federal responsibility are inclined sometimes to increase this value to justify a higher loan.
Now when this amount exceeds the limits set by the provincial government for the 3 per cent interest rebate, then the prospective owner of the house cannot benefit from the 3 per cent rebate which at the end of 20 or 25 years represents a very substantial amount.
I know that it may be difficult to adjust the federal and provincial legislation so that they may be complementary, but I feel that it is my duty to draw the attention of the minister to that point, especially to this advantage granted to the Quebec low wage earners to enable them to buy their own house.
That opportunity, which is offered to them by the provincial government, a reduction of interest is one that I should like the whole Canadian population to share. That is why I wonder, since there seems to be a definitive indication to move along their line, if the provincial opportunity offered at present by Quebec could not be extended to all Canadian citizens.
Could a federal measure not supplement that provincial legislation? Is such a move the responsibility of the provinces as far as the constitution is concerned? This is a point which can be argued upon, but if the federal government, which has more extensive credit powers than the provincial governments, if the government can, as it did today, in the proposals before us, vote, for instance, under item A, $100 million, under item F, $50 million and under item H, half a billion, for a total of $650 million, it certainly can extend that advantage to all the provinces. Then, I wonder about the ceiling on those amounts. Why $100 million, $50 million, $500 million. What are the true limits, since those credits apparently will be issued so that some people may build themselves houses, so that the corporation may back up loans and allow the municipalities to undertake planning and clearing projects in blighted areas. If the federal government is able to issue such credits, it certainly can, in my opinion, do without a portion of the 6 and 7 per cent interest it collects on those loans at the present time.
I am sure that they could be reduced in order to help the Canadian citizens, in order to allow small wage earners, in whom we are particularly interested-those earning $5,000 or less yearly-to become home owners.
However, the burden placed upon school boards and municipalities, which are compelled to raise their tax rates which have to be paid by the small home owner, defeats the very objective we have in mind.

In the province of Quebec especially, municipal taxes have doubled in the last three years. I know many persons who bought a home five or six years ago and who today are wondering whether to dispose of it or to deny themselves the bare necessities.
Mr. Chairman, that shows to what extent our provincial and municipal governments need sources of revenue precisely in order to assume their responsibilities. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to introducing legislation that would acknowledge the Canadian red ensign as Canada's distinctive national flag as endorsed by the Royal Canadian Legion and the I.O.D.E.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in bringing this motion before parliament I do so on behalf of those people who cannot speak for themselves in parliament except through the voices of their elected member or members.
When I placed this motion on the order paper last February I did not realize at that time that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson), come hell or high water, would rush the personal selection of his pennant to the stage where he was going to have his flag announced before my motion came up for debate. The views I wish to place on record this afternoon are my own personal views, as well as the opinions of approximately 90 per cent of the letters I have so far received from the people I represent-and naturally I am speaking of my own constituency, the riding of Elgin.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not speak for the Conservative party as a whole, for we on this side of the house are free thinkers and free speakers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SUGGESTED LEGISLATION ACKNOWLEDGING RED ENSIGN AS DISTINCTIVE NATIONAL FLAG
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SUGGESTED LEGISLATION ACKNOWLEDGING RED ENSIGN AS DISTINCTIVE NATIONAL FLAG
speechtext:
We are not like the Liberals who, on a Tuesday, were told by the Prime Minister, "When the flag question comes up for a vote it will be a free vote and you can vote as your conscience dictates," and then a few days later he changed that and made the statement that the government would stand or fall on the flag question. Oh yes, the Prime Minister says to his supporters, "It will be a free vote, but you vote for me and my flag-or else."
I do not know if the Prime Minister has as yet got himself on to that high water mark, but he sure has been getting heck from a lot of people who have expressed their opinions to me by telegram, mail and telephone. Universally public opinion, as I have received it, is, "Don't let Pearson throw our Canadian ensign into the garbage can." We wonder if the Prime Minister has forgotten that the red ensign really is the Canadian flag, as it was made so by order in council of September 5, 1945, P.C. 5888, signed by the Governor General, where it is ordered that-
-the red ensign with the shield of the coat-of-arms of Canada in the fly, (hereinafter referred to as the Canadian red ensign), may be flown from

buildings owned or occupied by the federal government within or without Canada-and that it shall be appropriate to fly the Canadian red ensign, within or without Canada, wherever place or occasion may make desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
Some weeks ago a question was placed on the order paper and eventually answered. It asked how many signatures the Prime Minister had so far received from persons who wished to have the Canadian ensign maintained as Canada's national flag. At the time of the reply, which was early in April, some
98,000	signatures had been received supporting the Canadian red ensign, and these were all of a voluntary nature. I am sure if a petition were widely circulated throughout Canada it would contain more names than were ever received by any government on any other matter, in support of our Canadian red ensign flag.
I have taken the opportunity to read the many letters appearing in the press from time to time, written by individuals concerning a Canadian flag. The great majority of these letters support the Canadian red ensign, and I am sure the writers have given this matter their serious consideration before writing to the editors of their respective papers.
The only distinctive flag for Canada is the present ensign and no other. It contains the union jack, which represents our union with the great commonwealth of nations. The coat of arms represents the four great peoples who discovered and built up Canada into one of the great nations of the world, the English, French, Irish and Scots. What more do we need for a distinctive flag?
In the last three wars over 100,000 of our finest citizens gave their lives for the defence of our ensign and what it represents. Does that not make it a distinctive flag? There are millions of fathers, mothers, wives, brothers, sisters and children mourning today for their loved ones who gave their lives that we should be free and not under a dictatorship. These people are proud of those who made the supreme sacrifice in upholding ensign and country. This also makes our ensign distinctive.
I agree that flag as it stands today may not be entirely acceptable to everyone in Canada, but I am equally certain it is acceptable to the majority of us who are proud to call it our flag. The flag is not only for display to Canadians in Canada, or simply to visitors to Canada; it is our symbol overseas in all countries and also in the United States and must, therefore, be a flag in accordance with the long accepted principles of heraldry and tradition.
Canadian Flag
Speaking on behalf of the Royal Canadian Legion and the ladies of the Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire, who have taken a definite stand on our flag question and universally adopted the Canadian red ensign, they have put forward, time and again, their stand to the Prime Minister and to members of parliament. Recently the annual Canadian Legion's convention in Winnipeg and the annual meeting of the I.O.D.E. again unanimously adopted the Canadian ensign as Canada's flag.
Of course, as we all know, the Prime Minister thought he would brave the lions in their own den and make an appearance at the annual meeting of the Royal Canadian Legion in Winnipeg to unveil to them his proposal for his new flag. I believe it is true that he was booed and cheered to some extent when he announced the proposal for a flag, but how otherwise could these 1,900 delegates raise an objection to a flag, other than the Canadian red ensign, before the Prime Minister of Canada when he was attending their meeting? Would each one of them have had the opportunity to express his individual views to the Prime Minister? No, Mr. Speaker.
It is interesting to note the words of Mr. C. B. Sinclair, second vice president of the Canadian corps association spoken last fall. He had this to say:
The time for a different flag might have been in 1867, at the time of confederation, but certainly not 1967, the one hundredth anniversary of confederation. The day is long gone when any federal government should consider tampering with our Canadian red ensign, with its long history and tradition. To do so now, would I think, be an attempt at political expediency of the lowest order. If the various "ethnic groups" which have migrated to Canada from other lands, and have become an integral part of our growing country are told with absolute and complete finality, that the Canadian red ensign is the flag of Canada, they will accept this as part of their new life, as happily and as completely as they accept all other aspects of their newly adopted country. Our present government and its immediate predecessor have been forced to function as minority governments, which is sometimes difficult, but we firmly believe in the maturity of the Canadian people, and, if our federal government can find the courage to govern wisely, with political considerations giving way to national necessities and wellbeing, the citizens of Canada, both new and old, would applaud such courage, and we could all look forward to 1967, when our nation will celebrate its one hundredth birthday, and with this centennial celebrated under the same flag as its birth-who could ask for greater consistency?
I feel the Prime Minister has left the impression with the people of Canada that the majority of his present mail favours a new flag. But I wish to place on the record a portion of a letter that he received and which I am sure neither he nor any of his supporters will be placing on the record for public scrutiny. It is from a resident in

Canadian Flag
my constituency who was kind enough to mail carbon copies of it both to myself and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker).
I was speaking to this gentleman yesterday and he said it was the first time he had ever written to any leader of any government, but he was so incensed when the announcement of a new flag for Canada was made that he had to sit down and put his feelings in a letter and direct it to the Prime Minister of Canada. This is a six page letter, but I am only going to deal with the first two pages which cover the flag question. It reads as follows:
St. Thomas, Ont.
May 16, 1964
Hon. Mr. Lester B. Pearson,
Prime Minister of Canada.
Dear Sir:
Regards your tenure of office as Prime Minister and your vaunted 60 days of decision which has turned out to be 300 days of indecision, I have listened to your interviews on television with Mr. DePoe and Mr. Pelletier and others and your own admission in the press that you have made many mistakes this term. I have always admired your abilities. But these interviews have been very disappointing. You give the Impression of a schoolboy trying to convince the teacher he has his homework done when he has not. Why all the sidestepping? If you don't change you may go down in history as the most destructive and incompetent prime minister Canada has ever had. Your inability to control the country. Why do you allow threats against the Queen? A good leader would make short work of the F.L.Q. and others. Regards your promise of a new flag for Canada. By what right as an individual have you to make a decision to change the flag of our country? Then push over on us one of no meaning. The maple leaves bud in the spring and die in the fall. What shall we cling to the rest of the year? Your explanation at Espanola, Ontario, to the Canadian Legion was very weak.
Your remarks of how proud we were in the first world war to wear the maple leaf on our uniforms. Yes, only denoted to other army personnel of other countries where we were from. They also had a mark of distinction on their uniforms. It was the red ensign that held us together. It was for that the boys bled and died for. Have you forgot 1892 when it was first used. The order in council by the cabinet in 1924. The federal order in council 1945. That the red ensign was the national flag for Canada. This is the flag of unity for all Canada. Mr. Prime Minister are you listening to the voices of the extremists for your own personal gain and trying to push over on the majority of this meaningless rag. In Ontario there is a town of Delhi on No. 3 highway. This community is largely made up of peoples of nationalities of every race of Europe as well as Canadians. They all live peaceably together. The different races speak their own tongues within themselves. Yet at the roadside of No. 3 highway they have a large red ensign encased in glass and Illuminated 24 hours a day. The inscription reads "This is our flag, let's keep it flying". This should be the motto for all Canada.
That is why these people came to Canada to be under that flag.

Since the end of the second world war in 1945, many persons from European countries have emigrated to Canada.

I think that we as members of parliament are all desirous of having unity within Canada. My question is this: Why the sudden rush for a new flag? What is wrong with our Canadian red ensign? It would appear that the Prime Minister and his government are
