subtopic: SUGGESTED LEGISLATION ACKNOWLEDGING RED ENSIGN AS DISTINCTIVE NATIONAL FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion that we have now before us deals with a subject in which a great many Canadians are interested at this time. I do not intend to engage in a broad discussion of this matter of a distinctive national flag; I will confine my remarks, pursuant to standing orders, to the content of this resolution which would have this government acknowledge the Canadian red ensign as the distinctive flag of Canada, as it is endorsed by the Royal Canadian Legion and the I.O.D.E. Although I completely agree with the principle of giving our country a distinctive national flag, and that as soon as possible, I cannot agree to this motion introduced by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. McBain) whereby this distinctive flag would be the red ensign on which we find the union jack and the coat of arms of Canada.
I am taking the liberty to add that, not only do I speak in my own name as a responsible member, but also for the people I represent, the people of Beauharnois-Salaberry county. I have met with my constituents during the last few days, and I feel quite free to express my views in the house.
I cannot see how we could consider that flag as really distinctive of our country while it shows the emblem of another country. Like many other Canadians, I have also learned to respect the Canadian red ensign and to accept its use during the last few years; but it has remained for me a pennant, an ensign, and not a flag meeting with the aspirations of a young and dynamic country.
It is a good thing that a flag should reflect our past but, on the other hand, it does not have to be a Canadian history book. We have the duty to select a flag which will really identify Canada and which, at the same time, will be an emblem that will make us look to the future, and a symbol of hope for our youth and future generations.
The union jack, in the upper left hand corner of the red ensign is, of course, a beautiful flag from an aesthetic point of view and it shows the origin of the British people by the superposition of the Cross of St. George, England's flag, the Cross of St.
Canadian Flag
Andrew, Scotland's flag, and the Cross of St. Patrick, Ireland's flag. However, the union jack has nothing Canadian, even though one third of the Canadian people are of British descent.
Our ancestors came to Canada to build a new country, a young country, a self-governing and independent country which, today, can assume its responsibilities in international affairs where its influence is well known. Therefore, Canada can and even must have a flag distinctive from that of any other country, showing that it is not under the dependence of any foreign or friendly nation.
I wish to offend nobody, but the red ensign still remains basically the flag of the British merchant marine, on which the coat of arms of Canada has been added. Only one fiftieth of the surface of the red ensign shows a really and purely Canadian identification, that is the three red maple leaves on white background which appear on the bottom part of the coat of arms of Canada.
From colonial states, our country achieved the status of a self-governing state. Then, it obtained its sovereignty and finally became one of the recognized nations of the world. This progressive and peaceful evolution took place without disrupting our relations with the motherlands of our founders. As this political evolution is now over, it is our duty to show it to the face of the world.
Why should the union jack instead of coat of arms of our country be in the foreground of a Canadian flag? Why should we not follow in respect of a national flag the same policy we started to implement, that is to strengthen Canadian thought, create a real Canadian image and, in a common effort towards understanding, unite Canadians from coast to coast.
Mr. Speaker, it is mentioned in the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Elgin that the Royal Canadian Legion and the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire are in favour of the adoption of the red ensign as a national flag.
So, before concluding my remarks, I will discuss this point, for I am a veteran who served under this flag, as a member of the Canadian air force during the last world war. I am also a regular member of the Canadian Legion, section 62, in Salaberry de Valleyfield.
I admit that the national directors of the Legion want us to maintain the red ensign as the Canadian flag. I did indeed go to Winnipeg for the opening of the convention, not only as a member of parliament, but as the delegate of my section, with a proxy when it came to the vote. I am far from being convinced that all the members of the legion in this country are in unanimous

Canadian Flag
agreement in this matter, and indeed, we have lately heard certain branches approving the Prime Minister when he submitted a distinctive national flag, on which there was no sign of allegiance to any other country. May I read to you the following letter addressed to me on May 12 by Mr. Larry Soly, chairman of local 62, in Valley-field,
Dear Gerald:
We ask our members' views with regard to the flag, and these were the results:
Red ensign: 30 per cent in favor.
Distinctive flag: 70 per cent in favor.
I hope that your stay in Winnipeg will be pleasant, and that you will find some time for rest.
You may use the two proxy votes of local 62, as you see fit. Dave Watson, our district representative, will also be at the convention, and he will certainly be pleased to meet you there.
Cordially,
Royal Canadian Legion 62
Larry Soly, Chairman.
Mr. Speaker, it is a significant fact that my section should have taken it upon itself to write this letter to me, without my having made any request in this respect, and should have given me its unlimited trust, whereas last November its members had had every opportunity of knowing my views on the flag question, when I had been invited as a speaker at their meeting. In Winnipeg, I also had an opportunity of discussing with several members of the Legion, from various parts of the country, and even there some were ready to accept a national flag which would be really distinctive, other than the red ensign, and also a certain number of others who were not fighting with such grim determination for the red ensign as might be gathered from the statements coming from that convention and the resolutions which were voted at the meetings. I also had an opportunity of meeting a few young students from Winnipeg with whom I discussed the matter of the flag, and the hon. member for Jacques-Cartier-La-salle (Mr. Rock) was able to see, like myself, that a great majority among them favoured a truly Canadian flag to replace the red ensign.
If I may, I will now quote a paragraph of the order in council of September 5, 1945 which authorized the flying of this red ensign as our national flag.

That, until such time as action is taken by parliament for the formal adoption of a national flag, it is desirable to authorize the flying of the Canadian red ensign on federal government buildings within as well as without Canada, and to remove any doubt as to the propriety of flying the Canadian red ensign wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.

As you can notice, the terms used:


That, until such time as action is taken by parliament for the formal adoption of a national flag-

That, until such time as action is taken by parliament for the formal adoption of a national flag.
Those words indicate that even at that time consideration was being given to the adoption of a truly distinctive flag and that the red ensign was to be used during the period of transition which would eventually lead us to choose a purely Canadian standard free from any foreign symbol. We have reached that historic moment which is an indication of our political maturity and of our national pride and the attachment we have for our country.
Consequently, I would ask the house to reject this motion which is contrary to the wishes of the majority in Canada and to give our people and our children as soon as possible a truly national identity through the adoption, by parliament, of a flag bearing the colours of Canada, that is three red maple leaves on a white background with a blue stripe at both ends.

subtopic: SUGGESTED LEGISLATION ACKNOWLEDGING RED ENSIGN AS DISTINCTIVE NATIONAL FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking briefly to the resolution before us I should like to say, first of all, that the opinions I express are my own. I do not know how it is in other parties in this house on this resolution or on the flag question generally, but in the New Democratic party we have decided to have a free vote-a free vote on this resolution and on the flag issue. Personally I believe this is a fair and very wise decision. A flag-the red ensign, as the resolution before us champions, or any other flag-is something which to me cuts across all party lines and all classes of opinion in the country. For example, there are some in my own party who favour the red ensign, as this resolution asks. There are those who oppose it and favour a distinctive, or a more distinctive, Canadian flag. Then there is a third group in my party, and I believe in some of the other parties in the house as well, which has a different opinion still. That opinion, and I voice it in relation to the resolution before us, as I would on any other flag resolution, is that the present government and the present house have no mandate from the Canadian people to decide the flag issue, either the red ensign or the proposed maple leaf flag.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that in the last election one of the parties, the Liberal party, proposed the establishment of a distinctive Canadian flag. However I think that most

hon. members would agree with me that this was never an issue in the campaign. It was seen in the Liberal party literature that they proposed a distinctive Canadian flag, but I am sure that many members here will agree with me that in the Liberal campaign literature in the past we have seen such proposals put forward as a medicare plan, which was suggested as early as 1919. I do not think that the majority of Canadians thought that the red ensign as proposed in the resolution before us, or the proposed new flag, would really be an issue in this House of Commons.
Personally, I think that if the present government or the present house, which is still made up of minorities, has any mandate from the people of Canada on the flag issue, that mandate would extend in my mind only to placing before the people of Canada what this resolution calls for, the red ensign, or a more distinctive Canadian flag, and of doing that in the form of a plebiscite, and urging the people of Canada to make their choice as to the emblem they wish.
I think that the introduction of the flag issue at this particular stage of the session, so far from unifying the country may have an adverse or even the opposite effect. In the meantime, while we are debating such resolutions as the one before us on the red ensign or the one on the general flag issue, we are surely taking up time which should be devoted to more pressing economic issues in the country. I also think that if we vote on this resolution tonight or on the more general flag resolution later, whatever settlement we make or whatever vote we come to will be decided on a majority basis. But that decision will not in any way remove the deep emotional feelings which the people of this country have in respect to the red ensign or to the general flag issue. Whether we vote it down or whether we vote in support of the red ensign or the proposed new flag, I do not think that that will be an end to the issue in the country. Here we are, 265 members of parliament out of a population of between 19 and 20 million people, a population which has never been really asked to give its opinion either for the red ensign or for this new flag. We are supposed to make a decision on this matter without damaging the unity of the country. I do not think that that is a practical proposition. I feel that, rather than voting on the resolution before us or on the government's coming resolution, we should consider very carefully whether it would not be better in the long run and in the interest of the country to take this matter out of party politics and to put before the people a plain plebiscite asking them to decide between the red ensign or the maple leaf flag. This is my own view, and it 20220-242J
Canadian Flag
is shared by some members of my party as well perhaps as by some members of other parties. I put it forward sincerely because I feel that the flag issue is one which will be much better handled in the way I suggest.
It is not too late for the present administration to take a second look at putting before us the flag proposal which they have in mind. They have earlier taken second looks at matters such as the sales tax, the budget and the pension plan. There is still time for a full reconsideration of this issue.
In conclusion, I would say that if we made up our mind to remove the issue from the house and from politics and to put it before the people in a plebiscite, we would then get the most democratic expression in the country of the people's will on the flag issue, and it would also enable us to get on with more pressing economic matters. So to that degree I oppose the resolution which is now before us.

subtopic: SUGGESTED LEGISLATION ACKNOWLEDGING RED ENSIGN AS DISTINCTIVE NATIONAL FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is strange to hear an N.D.P. member who must have new principles for a new democracy. When the majority has declared itself in favour of something they do not like, such as nuclear weapons and, in this case, the national flag, they claim that we must set little store by the vote of the people. But if, for various reasons, they feel we must respect the will of the people, they invoke the principles of true democracy and they speak of the operation of our democratic institutions. And they say it is irregular for members of parliament to pass legislation concerning the flag.
As the new distinctive flag project for Canada was contained in the platform of the party now in office, of the government party, I believe the members are entitled to represent the people who elected them and there is no question of holding a referendum or a plebiscite thereafter. The government takes a position, it makes a decision, and if democracy does not like this government's decision, the government may be overthrown in the next election.
But as this article was included in the platform of the Liberal party, I see absolutely no reason for holding a referendum or a plebiscite. Besides, it would take about 97 years thereafter for us to get a really distinctive flag.
And I come back to the motion before us. When it is said that the red ensign is a distinctive flag for Canada, I admit this is right, but I also believe it must be admitted the Canadian people today want an entirely and decidedly distinctive flag, and it is why the red ensign should not be recognized as a completely and absolutely distinctive flag.

Canadian Flag
The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. McBain) said that we celebrated the advent of confederation in 1867 with the red ensign and that we should also celebrate the centennial under the red ensign. I regret I have to differ with him, but surely the Canadian flag, which was accepted and adopted by order in council in 1945, did not exist in 1867 as the distinctive flag of Canada. Consequently, I am not ready to accept his argument on this point.
Mr. Speaker, I have before me Mr. Ollivier's book entitled British North America Acts and Selected Statutes, in which I find the Statute of Westminster, which was assented to on December 11, 1931. In the preamble, among other things, we read:
And whereas it is meet and proper to set out by way of preamble to this Act that, inasmuch as the crown is the symbol of the free association of the members of the British Commonwealth of Nations, and as they are united by a common allegiance to the Crown, it would beta accord...
Therefore, the Statute of Westminster, without referring to any flag whatever, neither the union jack nor any other, states in its preamble that we form part of the commonwealth of nations.
This is pointed out in the Statute of Westminster, in the preamble that was accepted by all the commonwealth countries at that time. Now I should like to quote section 11 of the Statute of Westminster. Here it is:
Notwithstanding anything in the Interpretation Act, 1889, the expression "Colony" shall not, in any Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom passed after the commencement of this Act, include a Dominion or any Province or State forming part of a Dominion.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, the Statute of Westminster, which was accepted not only by the provinces of the dominion but by the parliament of the United Kingdom as well, clearly provided that thereafter Canada and the other commonwealth countries were no longer colonies.
I believe it is reasonable that the people of a colony be keen on showing, some way or other, their dependence on the mother country. But when the colony no longer exists, when it has clearly and definitely achieved independence, I do not think it is an indication of pride to be bent on showing in a flag any sign of dependence. I think that what proved to be an obstacle for some time to the adoption of a really distinctive flag, is the fact that my fellow countrymen speaking another language would have liked it very much if French Canadians had insisted on some little sign showing their feelings towards France. Well, we do not want any. Not because we are prejudiced against France or our feelings for France have diminished in any way, but because we believe that Canada is a full-grown country and that there is no
[Mr. Marcoux.l
reason why we should insist on some symbol of France on our flag.
And when we think we are practising Canadian nationalism, we think that we might resemble the Canadians who wanted our country to identify itself as a separate entity of North America, and not as an appendage or an appendix to a European country.
I happen to have here the House of Commons Debates for 1935, which I took for another reason, and where I read a speech by Henri Bourassa, who was one of the promoters of Canadian nationalism, not French Canadian, narrow or provincial, but a sound nationalism, a nationalism which makes us, French Canadians, think that it is a tragedy, like a new Dunkirk, to see a company like the Canadian Oil, for instance, sold to American interests, or John Labatt, sold to another American company; it grieves us, French Canadians, not because it is English capital that goes to the United States, but because it is Canadian capital which leaves us and goes to a foreign country.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, in the matter of a really distinctive flag, I do not think that we would be justified in accepting the red ensign. I agree that it was accepted in 1945, as I said a while ago, but we must not forget that in 1947 the Canadian parliament decided that Canadians could now avail themselves of the Canadian citizenship. We are now Canadian citizens, we are no longer British subjects, and I think that we should be proud to be Canadian citizens. If one must be proud to be a Canadian citizen, I feel one must also be proud to have a flag which clearly indicates that we are Canadian citizens and not British subjects or even French subjects.
The red ensign was used by our merchant navy; before, it had been used by the British merchant navy, and we added to it the Canadian coat of arms. Without discrediting the merchant navy which is practically non-existent today, the Canadian merchant navy has practically disappeared-even if it were still in existence, I feel that it would not be normal to accept an emblem belonging to it, that is belonging to a small group to give it to a much more important group such as the whole of Canada. It would not be normal, for instance, to take the flag of a province and have it adopted by the whole of Canada; it would neither be logical nor normal.
For the same reasons, I do not think that we should accept the flag of the merchant navy, even with the coat of arms of Canada added to it.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not go further. I speak for myself but I think I represent at least part of the members of my party. We also decided to have a free vote, not a vote

according to our conscience, because we always vote according to our conscience, but a free vote enabling the House of Commons to take an appropriate decision. That is not a decision to be taken through a plebiscite or some way other than the one brought forward.
Since the Prime Minister's motion is not being discussed, I shall not discuss it either. It may be that some hon. members will wish to discuss it to make some political capital, but personally, I am discussing the motion before the house and I say that I am against it, because I am too proud of being a Canadian, and a Canadian in North America.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the time of the five o'clock adjournment I had been paying my respects to the late Jack Garland and the late Stewart Bates. I can say, without any hesitation at all, that having listened for many years to the late Jack Garland, when he sat on this side of the house discussing his particular study and project relating to housing, we all felt assured that from his position on the ministerial benches there would be great advances made in the National Housing Act, there would be progressive measures introduced, and that there would be a new impetus and drive given to the organization which we know as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It is to be regretted that he is not here to give us of his vision of a new and expanded act, and to give of his drive to central mortgage and housing.
I firmly believe that there are needs for vital changes in the National Housing Act, that there is a great need for a new drive in central mortgage and housing. In speaking on this resolution I want first to make it clear that the major views of our party in this house have already been expressed by the hon. member for Greenwood. However there are one or two matters upon which I would like to speak briefly this evening.
I have always been a supporter of the underlying principles that motivated the organization of central mortgage and housing. I have always been a strong supporter of the National Housing Act, and I will continue to be a supporter of both the act and the organization, but I do feel the time has come for us to take a new look at the organization itself.
I believe that it is becoming somewhat moribund; that it is being engulfed in too much red tape; that it is wallowing in a pit of detail; that its vision does not extend

National Housing Act
very much beyond its organizational nose; that architecturally it looks along straight lines and some of its construction, especially in apartments, reminds me of upturned wooden crates with too much emphasis on straight line architectural theories, instead of the modern curve and crescent.
I feel, sir, that it is wallowing so much in detail, red tape, and lack of vision, that progress that could have been made during the past year or 18 months has not been made, and no commencement is even envisaged in the near future on projects which should now be nearing completion.
I was most interested in the remarks of the minister this afternoon when he was speaking of the responsibility of municipalities, of the need for clearing slums and for new development. When he said that it gave me the perfect example of what I have in mind, when I was reminded of his own constituency of Vancouver Centre. With all due honour to the wonderful people who reside in the four to six blocks east of Main street -the minister I know will agree-though a certain start was made in that area, there is a great deal to be done and if there ever was an area where the bulldozer should go in- and should have gone in years ago-it is right in that area at the eastern end of the minister's constituency.
I am convinced from my own knowledge, and I feel certain the minister must feel the same way, that a start could have been made there a year or 18 months ago. He knows, as I know, that the residents in that area were prepared to do something. They wanted to co-operate with the municipality, the province and central mortgage and housing. At their own expense they hired an architect and drafted plans. They submitted their plans to the city, to the province and to central mortgage and housing, yet month after month went by and no start was made, although the money was there as well as the plans.
I personally made a visit down here to Ottawa to see central mortgage and housing about this development, and I can only say that it was the red tape, the detail, the lack of co-operation here in Ottawa that have caused the stalemate on that project-and unnecessarily from my point of view, and I think from the point of view of the residents themselves. Now we have a proposition that in future, perhaps, they can go ahead with this plan, which would have been of terrific benefit to Vancouver because it would have meant a development primarily of a two-section block area, but eventually of a four-section block area of modern construction. The oriental touch however, would be kept side by side with the business Chinatown of Vancouver,

so as to provide new homes for the thousands of our Chinese Canadians who live in the area and a tourist attraction unparalleled in Canada, with the second largest Chinatown on the North American continent. Yet this plan has been held up, for no reason, as far as I have been able to ascertain from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, though the people are ready not only with the plans but with the money from trust funds.
Now we hear of a redevelopment plan for the Chinatown in this area and I am most pleased to have received a letter from Mr. Graham who is director of planning for the city of Vancouver under date of April 10. He says:
The final scheme produced was a compromise from the original submission by the Vancouver Chinatown development association. It still had the same unique oriental environment but eliminated technical problems which violated many principles laid down by city council for all development.
You may not be aware, but the V.C.D.A. group will be given an apportunity to participate in town house development elsewhere in the redevelopment area and there is no reason why this should not have the same oriental aspect as their original scheme.
In view of the fact that we now have a submission from the director of planning of the Vancouver planning department which is going to meet the desires of the Canadian Chinese in this area of Vancouver, a plan which, I understand, has met with the approval of the Vancouver city council, I certainly hope there is to be no further delay on the part of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and I sincerely hope this will tie in with the simultaneous development of the Chinese business district. I feel the minister has the same sense of pride as I have in this wonderful group of Chinese Canadians which is shared between his constituency and mine. I know he will be glad to see that these citizens, who were prepared to move two years ago with regard to housing development, are issuing a challenge to their own people to move ahead with the business development. I was interested to read in the Chinatown News of May 18 an editorial on the front page which is a challenge to its readers and an example to people elsewhere who live under conditions such as those under which these people have, unfortunately, been living for so many years. It says:
Now that the Vancouver city planning department has come up with concrete proposals to rejuvenate Chinatown, will our businessmen and property owners seize this opportunity to embark on a major rebuilding scheme?
Among the community minded citizens we have talked to, many are genuinely alarmed over the steady decline of Pender St. as evidenced by the growing number of restaurants forced to curtail their hours of operation Or go out of business altogether. What is the answer?

We need more tourists. One way to attract them is keep this area growing. In other words, revitalize Chinatown. This can only be achieved by a major renovating or rebuilding job.
The suggestion might sound drastic, but a start will have to be made somewhere. The time is here and now.
The writer points out that they have the architects and are familiar with what is being done in San Francisco and Honolulu, along these lines. So they are prepared to move, and I, for my part, am requesting that we see a little more life and activity-a little more co-operation from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in moving along the lines proposed by the people in this area, so that something may be done not only to rebuild the area and construct new homes there but to bring into being a new business centre as well.
Speaking of construction, I recall the remarks of the minister this afternoon to the effect that municipal control is necessary to stop structural deterioration. I want to express the hope that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will see to it that new construction is of such a nature that there will not be deterioration. I think the specifications which are now followed by that corporation are an absolute disgrace. I worked for the construction industry for many years, and one of my major tasks was the reading of specifications, regulations and blueprints. For the life of me I cannot figure out how contractors who work with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, or how inspectors of that corporation can make head or tail of the regulations and specifications in that little book which contractors are supposed to follow and which the inspectors are supposed to enforce. It is bad enough reading the specifications, but when one has to read amendments to the specifications and then read amendments to the amendments to the amendments of the specifications, heaven only knows how one is supposed to build a house. I do not know who draws up these regulations and I cannot for the life of me figure out who approves them, because they are a disgrace to the whole construction industry.
I speak as one who has worked most of his life in that industry. I do not know how some of these homes stand up. It is amazing to me why the first floor does not collapse, having regard to the new regulations as to the spacing and the size of joists. If it were not for the spreaders, I think they would collapse. I have been over many of these homes. I have read through the specifications and regulations time after time and they certainly lay down the poorest building code I have come across in my whole life. My own home, built 54 years ago, was better constructed than homes constructed today under these
National Housing Act
regulations. So let us not tear down slums for the purpose of putting up homes which will be slums themselves in a few years. I ask most sincerely that not only shall we have vision and action with regard to new home and apartment construction but that our regulations shall make sure they are modern and well built. That is the responsibility of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I should like to see more initiative shown by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under the National Housing Act in the construction of homes and apartments for the aged in Canada. In the past few years big strides have been taken in this field, but they still do not deal adequately with this problem. One can visit these homes and apartments for the aged and find that for each one there is a waiting list hundreds long. Some have been waiting, not months but years, to get the comfort of a home or apartment in their declining days, at a rate they can afford to pay, so as to live in decency as the pioneers of this country. I feel strongly on this matter as one closely associated with my late father who initiated the first senior citizens housing project in Canada. When we speak of subsidized housing and low rental housing I fear we are not giving enough thought to the needs of the senior citizens of this country and I hope the vision and the dream which I know was in the mind of the late Jack Garland will not be allowed to disappear. I trust that, to revere his memory the government will bring in, if they have not already the authority, a measure to give them the power to provide an impetus to the construction of homes for our senior citizens.
That was all I wanted to add to the very wonderful address given by the hon. member for Greenwood this afternoon. I want to conclude by saying that wishful thinking is not enough; generalities are not enough; good intentions are not enough; legislation which is on the statute books is not enough. We require a vital, vigorous and farsighted central mortgage and housing administration. I hope we will be getting it in the future, and if we do not see signs of real activity in the immediate future perhaps we will have to place a bomb under them; and the best bomb I can think of would be either a special committee or a committee of this house composed of those who have a vital interest in housing, and those who know and understand construction. Then we could let them go at both the act and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I say this, Mr. Chairman, because security does not mean very much to the people of this country unless they have comfortable homes and comfortable apartments in which to live, at prices they can afford to pay.

National Housing Act [Translation]

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution deals with certain amendments the government wants to make to the National Housing Act under which the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was set up in 1954.
We feel that those amendments are not only necessary but urgent and that the government could have extended the list of paragraphs which appear in the resolution under consideration.
Mr. Chairman, when C.M.H.C. was established in 1957, it was to benefit the workers and small farmers, in other words it was to help the small man build himself a home.
C.M.H.C. has helped in the construction of housing centres in several parts of Canada, in Montreal, Quebec city, Toronto, Ottawa, Hull, in the larger cities and even in certain small communities, but with quite a bit of trouble.
It does not seem to be interested, for instance, in going too far in the Lake St. John and Abitibi areas, or in northern Ontario. Some work was done a few years ago in the Elliot Lake area, which is represented by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson). We have seen the results of these buildings and housing centres in Elliot Lake, as we will soon see them in Bancroft. We are witnessing the casting aside of small properties which were valued at $12,000, $15,000 or $18,000 at the time they were built. If we go to Elliot Lake today, we see these nice little houses-gems of houses indeed-with the windows boarded up. People are not living in them because they had to leave in order to earn their living elsewhere since Elliot Lake was closing its mines.
In other cities, in Montreal for instance, thousands of houses were built without proper consideration. If you go to St. Vincent de Paul today you will see hundreds of empty houses. Why? Not because the plant workers do not want to live in them but because payments are too high for an ordinary family. When a worker can pay $50 or $60 a month for rent and the houses built under C.M.H.C. come to $125, $135 or $150 a month, it is not surprising then to see a great number of empty houses.
The amendments to the 1954 act do not seem to do much to help the average family, with an average income, who cannot inhabit one of those houses.
Paragraph (a) concerns mainly the provinces and municipalities. The resolution provides:
That it is expedient...
(a) to provide further assistance to provinces and municipalities carrying out urban renewal programs by authorizing Central Mortgage and

Housing Corporation (hereinafter referred to as "the corporation") to make contributions and loans to provinces or municipalities to assist them in meeting the costs of such programs, and for the purpose to provide for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of amounts not exceeding in the aggregate one hundred million dollars:
What can the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation do with $100 million for all of Canada at this time, when the municipalities are contending with huge debts? Will this help the municipalities to pay their debts or, at least, to pay the interest on their debt which now takes up 40 and even 60 per cent of their annual budget?
Does the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation want to help the municipalities by making them sink deeper and deeper into a debt which they are unable to repay by demanding exorbitant carrying charges or interests?
Mr. Chairman, this may be a temporary help for the municipality, but in future we shall again be faced with the same situation as now; there will be absolutely no change. This may, for the time being, help give work to the unemployed in our municipalities. That is, no doubt, the minister's aim when he puts his name to such a resolution: to help relieve unemployment in this country and allay distress, by making loans to the municipalities for periods of 20, 25 and 30 years.
Suppose a municipality borrows $550,000 for 25 years at 5i or 6 per cent. In 25 years, that municipality will have to pay back almost $3.5 million for a $550,000 loan made this year, that is, it will have to pay three times the amount in 25 years.
Of course, 25 years from now it is likely that most members of parliament will no longer be sitting in this house because they will have disappeared, but our children, who will then pay the capital and interest, will probably wonder, and rightly so, if their parents were intelligent or if they suffered from a terrible lack of grey matter between their ears? If we are still here 25 years from now, we will probably hear such remarks. Why? Because we continue with the same system.
The government probably thinks that it is helping municipalities. If it sincerely wants to help municipalities, there is nothing at all, no federal legislation which prevents the minister from acting along those lines. By using the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, it could supply funds created by the Bank of Canada without interest for

municipalities, so that when we build a sidewalk, we will not have to pay for two sidewalks, one for the finance company and one for the people who use it.
When we build a road, when we pave a city street, or when we improve municipal services, we should not have to pay twice the price of those services, once for the finance company and once for the users of those services.
This resolution will get us nowhere. I understand that the whole financial or monetary system is faced with concern and uncertainty. We must pass and approve such a resolution so that the bill can be introduced as soon as possible.
As I said, the present problem will not be solved for the provinces or the municipalities, regardless of the intention of this resolution presented to us today. In that resolution, it is also proposed, in paragraph (b):
To authorize the corporation to make loans and to ensure loans made by approved lenders to owners of existing houses in areas included in urban renewal programs.
There again, it is the same thing. The act will be extended so that people who own houses which have been occupied can sell them with the financing of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or of insurance companies to be guaranteed by C.M.H.C., which is a crown corporation.
In paragraph (c):
To authorize the corporation to make loans and contributions to provincially or municipally owned housing agencies...
To assist individuals or families of low income.
What does that mean? As I said a while ago, in 1954, that is exactly ten years ago, it was said and repeated that low rent and low cost houses would be built. Today, we realize that the rent of those houses is $80, $85 or $90. When the instalment payable to the corporation or to the insurance company does not go up, municipal taxes double, school taxes triple or quadruple as we have seen in so many places in the province of Quebec. Then, everything is added up to make a monthly assessment which increases the cost of rents every six months, and, after six, eight or 15 years of payments on a house, we now see people who bought a small home in 1954 unable to face their liabilities any longer, just because municipal taxes have doubled and school taxes trebled or gone up five times their former amount.
Those people are today destitute, after having for six, eight and even 15 years, made payments or paid rent with regard to those small houses, believing that they would one day be the owners of a modest home. After
National Housing Act
ten years of work, the man who was 30 when he bought his home, is now 40 years old and, if he happened to lose his job, or were to experience financial stress, after having invested all his life's work and all his savings in his property to settle his wife and children in their own home, he would be without shelter.
Now, in 1964, the government introduces some amendments to the act to help those people remain in their own home, and others in the same circumstances or conditions. But will that fill the purse of the family head who is 40 or 45, at this time, and has trouble finding employment? That is the kind of security all those bills or amendments are bringing to the Canadian workers, to human beings in Canada.
Paragraph (d) is to help housing projects to include hotels or boarding houses or homes for older citizens and others.
In paragraph (e), it is proposed to authorize the corporation to make once more loans to families of low income. It is about what we find in paragraph (c), or about the same aim.
In paragraph (g) the resolution proposes:
to authorize the corporation to make loans to provinces to assist in the construction or expansion of sewage treatment projects and to authorize the corporation to forgive repayment of 25 per cent of the principal and interest-
Here, I believe the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as well as the government, could include in paragraph (g) the following: "to assist also in the expansion of hospitals not only in this province but also in the whole of Canada, and especially as concerns the province of Quebec". For instance, to provide the provinces with the necessary funds to expand hospitals; indeed, there is a need for additional hospital beds throughout the province of Quebec. Why is there a shortage of beds? Why is it not possible to expand those hospitals? It is always for the same reason: the provincial government has no money, it is like the United Nations, it cannot even meet its commitments.
The provincial government is grappling with an exceedingly urgent problem in the hospital field. Why not allow the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to provide the provinces with funds at a nominal interest rate, using funds created by the Bank of Canada? Because here, again, if we have in Canada the physical means, if we have the minds, the brainpower to build something, why do the government and the ministers not order the Bank of Canada to make financially possible what the Canadian nation can do and is able to realize materially in Canada for the general welfare of the population?

National Housing Act
In paragraph (h), the resolution proposes:
to increase from two billion dollars to two and one half billion dollars the maximum charge on the consolidated revenue fund for direct loans by the corporation;
From $2 billion to $2.5 billion. Another financial game. Physical possibilities are not taken into account. The needs which actually exist in Canada are not considered. We lose a great deal of time here, in this house, on all sorts of questions, without attempting to find a solution to the main problem, which is that of finance in Canada. This is what ails everybody, including the government.
I am quite convinced that the government would be willing, if it had the financial possibilities, to help the people as a whole, the unemployed, the mothers whose families are in need, as well as those who are hungry and thirsty for justice in Canada. But the government is not taking the means to serve the purpose for which economic policies are set up, that is the human being.
In paragraph (1):
to provide for the establishment of a special account in the consolidated revenue fund out of which amounts not exceeding in the aggregate one hundred million dollars-
One hundred million dollars. Money again. Always money, from start to finish. That is the question. But where will C.M.H.C. obtain those funds? It is being said and suggested most clearly: C.M.H.C. will underwrite finance companies, insurance companies, lenders who may or may not be recognized today but will be tomorrow; it will underwrite them in respect of the loans granted.
Once again it is a poultice on a wooden leg. It will not cure the ill. It will only spread it. It will only entrench it and confirm it for another five years, because in five years the government-it may be that the present government will no longer be there but will have been replaced by another which will have to make new amendments to those amendments submitted to us in June 1964, because those amendments will not solve the problem.
I see that my good friends opposite are shaking their heads. They will have to open their wallets five years from now and they will find that I was right about what I am saying tonight in this connection. They are mistaken and they know it.

Do not deceive yourself, you will no longer be here in five years, not with that.
Mr. Chairman, this legislation will not solve the problem. The government merely goes around the difficulty and covers it with chocolate as one does with a pill. One day, the people will come to realize the bitterness of a financial system which is not adapted to the true possibilities of our country.
Let the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have the power, indeed let it be ordered to use without interest the money created by the Bank of Canada, and then not only C.M.H.C., small house owners, industrialists, municipalities or the provinces, but all the people will get a dollar's worth for every dollar borrowed from the corporation. That is what we want. We advocate a happy equilibrium between the monetary system and our physical potential I see that the minister is looking at me. As long as we do not adopt such a monetary policy to make financially possible in Canada what is physically desirable, we will be running around in a circle and we will be losing our time as the minister is bound to find out within a few years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we heard the minister's opening speech explaining the policy of the government, or at least what seemed to be the policy of the government. I think it is a sad commentary on the attitude in our country today that when we are discussing what I believe could be one of the most important programs yet put forward by this government or by any government, if this government means business as the minister seemed to indicate, we have had in the press gallery one, and at the moment, two reporters furnishing the news to the public. This afternoon at five o'clock when we were discussing a resolution having to do with the flag-and I am not suggesting for a moment that the flag is not an important issue-there were a dozen or more reporters in the press gallery.
I am not being too critical of the press, Mr. Chairman, because the press is a rather good mirror of public opinion. Unfortunately the public are not very interested in this subject. After all, we have bought the image which has been sold to us by the image makers, the public relations people, and we like to think we live in an affluent society in this country. We do, in so far as housing is concerned, if we happen to be fortunate enough to be earning $6,000 a year or up. If you can afford to pay $15,000 for a house, if you can afford to pay $100 or $150 a month rent for an apartment, you have no difficulty.

There are hundreds of apartments in Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg or Vancouver which can be rented tonight if you can pay that amount of money.
However, Mr. Chairman, if you are unfortunate enough to be earning $50 per week or if you are unfortunate enough to have four or five children and you have to live in one of the many slums or semi-slums which are a blight on the face of every city in this country, then of course you are out of luck. The majority of people and, I am afraid the majority of the members of this parliament, are not very interested. We have done an excellent job of building hundreds of thousands of homes in Canada since the end of world war II. But what have we built for the people who really need assistance? What have we built in the way of subsidized, low rental housing units? We have built less than 10,000.
I should like to think the minister's speech indicated a new policy and that the resolution outlined a real program that would be pushed ahead. We have lived with this kind of policy ever since world war II. The act, as it has been up until now, has not been a bad one. If you compare it with the legislation in European countries or in the United States, it is not much worse. Yet, these other countries have been able to build houses for the people who really need them, while we have done virtually nothing. One of the reasons we have done virtually nothing, Mr. Chairman, is that the federal government has merely prepared an act and said to the provinces or municipalities, "Yes, we are prepared to help; yes, the money is there". The federal government has been prepared to pay a substantial part of the subsidies required for financing housing units for people who cannot afford to pay an economic rent themselves. Having done that, the federal government has forgotten all about it.
What we will not face up to is the fact that in most provinces the provincial governments have shown very little interest. In most cities, I think I could say in all cities, the city councils are to a large extent made up of men who come from the professions of law, insurance, or real estate. I speak with some knowledge on this matter, having served on the Winnipeg city council and having attended a number of conferences of mayors and municipalities. These members represent on the city council those people who have already purchased their own houses and who are already living quite comfortably. So we tend to ignore the people who just cannot afford to pay for decent accommodation. It is easy to drive away from this building, to drive down Carling avenue and quickly get to the west end where the new housing
National Housing Act
developments are located. We ignore the fact that two blocks off Wellington one can see houses-I should not call them houses-one can find accommodations which are a disgrace in a country that has the wealth of Canada.
The minister gave some statistical information in his speech the other day. I should like to enlarge on some of the figures which he used. I have taken these illustrations from the 1961 census figures. Of the 4.5 million homes that we have in Canada, over 400,000 have only cold water facilities; over 200,000 of these are in the city. Almost 400,000 homes have no installed bath or shower, and 168,000 of these are in urban areas. This is in the year 1964, in a country that has the wealth of Canada, a country which has all the resources needed to provide homes for the people. Of the 4.5 million homes, over 200,000 in urban areas have shared toilet facilities which are shared by two or more households. Of the 4.5 million houses over a million and a half were built before 1920 and therefore, in most cases, need major repairs. Of the 3i million urban homes, over 900,000 were built before 1920.
In my own province, almost one third of the urban homes were built before 1920. We do not have the brick houses that you have in eastern Canada, so many of these homes need major repairs. Of the 4.5 million homes in Canada, only three million are heated by a furnace while a million and a half are heated by stoves, space heaters or less. Of the 3i million homes in urban areas, over
750,000	were heated by a stove, a space heater or worse. If you look at the refrigeration facilities, you see the same situation. Almost 400,000 homes have no refrigeration facilities at all. Of the 3| million urban homes, over 100,000 have no refrigeration facilities.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is easy to get lost in statistics. When one talks about a million homes, he tends to forget the individual case. We have heard from the member for Greenwood, from the member for Vancouver East and from the minister about some of the conditions in which some of the people in this country live.
My own city of Winnipeg is far from being the worst, but I wish that all members of parliament could have a look at some of the conditions which we permit to exist at this time. I know the minister has had the chance to do so.
A couple of years ago a Winnipeg newspaper carried an article dealing with the conditions. They listed the fact that in one home, of many which they visited, the only way in which the rats could be kept out was by boarding up the holes through which they

National Housing Act
came. They pointed out that children had been seen playing in houses condemned a year or more ago by the city but which had not been pulled down and had been seen coming out of these condemned houses swinging rats by the tail.
A family of seven lived in a house 12 feet wide which had only two tiny bedrooms. The father, mother and one baby slept in one bedroom and the other four children slept in the other bedroom, three of them sleeping in one bed. They had to live in that kind of house, of course, because the father was only making $200 a month and the most he could afford to pay for rent, unless the family cut down on its food bill, was $50 a month. So this was the kind of house in which they were living. Around the comer there were two families living in three rooms, with no closets, no bathtubs, no hot water.
In a survey made of one of Winnipeg's oldest areas in 1960, and I use this survey because nothing has been done to improve conditions in that area since, the welfare council of greater Winnipeg found that of 309 residential buildings only 1.76 per cent could be classified as being in good condition, 25.6 per cent in fair condition, 27.2 per cent in poor condition and 45.26 per cent in very poor condition. According to the report, in the same area 20 per cent of the houses have toilets shared by more than six people, 27 per cent have no baths, 32 per cent have no washbasins and 34 per cent are heated only by stoves.
Finally, after years of the kind of haggling to which the hon. member for Vancouver East has just referred, after years of planning and discussions between the city of Winnipeg, the province of Manitoba, the government of Canada and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a beginning has been made in the city of Winnipeg. The first redevelopment project in Winnipeg is now under way. As a matter of fact, the minister has issued an invitation, which I and other members from Winnipeg will certainly accept, to go to Winnipeg toward the end of the month for the official opening. I have had the opportunity of seeing the houses in which the people were living, and they were living under the same kind of conditions which I have already described, although I was referring to a different area in which no redevelopment is yet planned. I have also had the opportunity of seeing the housing units into which these people are moving.
I could criticize the plans which were made; I could criticize some of the details of the new project, but it is a fantastic improvement for the people who are moving in there. But, Mr. Chairman, let us face the fact that this housing project of which I am speaking,

which the minister has mentioned and of which we can all be proud, will only house a couple of hundred families. When you realize that Winnipeg has literally thousands of substandard units, to say that we in Winnipeg have finally begun to meet the problem by rehousing a couple of hundred families is merely to indicate that we have barely begun, and how little we have done to meet the problems which face us.
In the redevelopment area in which close to 2,000 people had been living most of the houses were over 50 years old. A house built in 1839 to accommodate two people was found in a recent survey to be housing seven. A house that had a single family back in the early 1900's was occupied by three families with a total of 16 people. Of the 337 families in the area, 129 had five or more children and most lived in cramped, poor quarters, some without bathtubs and hot water.
Such was the shortage that tenants in rooming houses in these areas were taking in roomers. A high percentage of the people there, who were by no means paying low rents, were receiving welfare assistance. In other words, the people of Canada through their municipal, provincial and federal governments were and are in fact subsidizing slum landlords. This is true in every city in Canada. It is true of Ottawa; it is true of Montreal; it is true of Toronto; it is true of Vancouver. This is something of which we should all be thoroughly ashamed. As I have said the accommodation they are moving into is fantastically better.
A very good reporter in the city of Winnipeg wrote an article in the Winnipeg Tribune of December 28 last in which he describes the contrast and I should like to read a couple of paragraphs. He says:
Next spring Mr. and Mrs. E. are going to plant
flowers in front of their home-All their married
life they had lived in the slums of Jarvis ave. Two months ago they moved to the city's first low rental housing development at Burrows-Keewatin. In the slums the snow is grey with dirt and grime from crowded living. At their new home the snow is as clean as the neighbourhood.
In front of their apartment is a wide expanse of sod, waiting for the shrubs and trees in the spring. At their old home their five children were strangers to grass and flowers. It had no yard and the front boulevards were ground to dirt from use__
At Jarvis the lights are naked bulbs, with cords hanging from the ceiling. Mrs. E. needed no more persuading. Their apartment has two storeys and a basement. There are three bedrooms. The kitchen is bright and efficient with new equipment and ample cupboards. It is not elaborate, for an eye was kept on costs. But there is nothing of the appearance of cheap row housing. It has an air of solidity. And it has more breathing space outdoors than many commercial blocks.
I could go on, Mr. Chairman, but I think I have indicated what can be done and what

the minister talked about so eloquently the other day. But how many units of this type have we built in this great country? I have already mentioned that Winnipeg is just building its first project for less than 200 families, and we need several thousand. I doubt that we have built 10,000 public housing units altogether in Canada, despite the fact that we probably need 200,000 units in our cities alone.
We are doing almost as bad a job in the field of supplying adequate housing for our old people. Tens of thousands of our old people are living in the central parts of the cities of Canada in single rooms. They are cooking on a hot plate and reading by that little naked bulb which hangs from a cord in the centre of the ceiling.
We have seen what can be done. The service organizations and the Legion branches should be given a great deal of credit for the work they have initiated in every city in Canada, for the units they have built in which old people in receipt of old age pensions can live at a relatively modest rent. They are to be congratulated and the government which encourages this should be thanked; but when you compare what has been done with the existing needs we can see how little we have actually done.
It has been estimated in my own city that despite the efforts of the service clubs and the Legion we have accommodated just 700 of the 4,200 people who need special accommodation, and for the rest we are still giving them the kind of talk which the minister gave us this afternoon.
I do not want to be too critical of Toronto, as probably half the public housing units built in Canada are in Toronto; but if you compare what has been done in Toronto with what has been done in the United States, really it puts us to shame. I say this, even though we in Canada like to think the Americans are pretty callous and business minded, and we do not like to follow their lead in everything.
For the past four years Toronto has been talking about redeveloping the tumbledown section south of Queen street, opposite the new city hall. In the same period of time the city of Hartford has spent almost $45 million redeveloping a similar downtown area. Boston, which has a population about the same size as Toronto, has a 300 man redevelopment staff, while Toronto has a staff of just four people. In New Haven, which is about a quarter the size of Toronto, they have allocated 1,000 acres for redevelopment. That is as if Toronto had tackled the whole area bounded by Bathurst, Yonge, Bloor and
National Housing Act
Queen Streets. In Baltimore one in every five houses in that city has been marked for redevelopment.
Similarly, if one goes to Europe and looks at Great Britain, Sweden or any of the other western European countries, he can see projects for housing tens of thousands of people, projects which make ours look absolutely sick.
I was happy to hear the minister's speech and I am looking forward to having a chance to examine the bill in detail. But I suggest to the minister, and to the government, that the best bill in the world will not do the job which is required because too many of the provinces and the cities have wanted to ignore the problem. They seem to feel that if they ignore it, it will go away by itself. The minister can have the best bill in the world, and have virtually unlimited money available, but if it is only theoretical it will not accomplish very much.
If we are going to get on with the job of clearing out the slums, putting the people in the low income groups and the people who have reached retirement age into the kind of houses we would like to see them in, then it will be the job of the minister, his deputy, and central mortgage and housing to explain to the public, to the provincial governments and to the cities of Canada what can be done, what needs to be done, what should be done; and to explain how little this will cost in money, and certainly how little it will cost in comparison to the ills which are the results of the ignoring of horrible housing conditions which has gone on all these years.
I hope we will give less thought to the housing of people in the upper income brackets, people about whom the hon. member for Greenwood spoke, because they have been able to get housing accommodation and will be able to get it. It is time we thought about the people who need housing and who, until now and under previous governments, have been almost completely ignored.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
while we are at the resolution stage of a measure to amend the National Housing Act, I would like to make a few remarks in order to help families who may take advantage of this act. Indeed, one can say that up to now, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is an organization that has rendered prominent services to Canadians. In fact, I have had the opportunity of taking advantage of it myself, and I have been very pleased with it. Nevertheless, there are surely many improvements that could be made to this act.
3820	HOUSE OF COMMONS
National Housing Act
First of all, I would like to call the attention of the minister responsible for the administration of this corporation to the fact that there is only one French Canadian on its board of directors.
I do not think that is being fair to French Canadians, who represent 30 per cent of the Canadian population. I suggest there is room for improvement there, because it is not by giving them one member out of ten that we are giving French Canadians a fair deal.
Mr. Chairman, I notice also that the balance sheet shows an accumulated reserve in the mortgage insurance fund, etc., of $122,440,000. And, once again, I do not think the main purpose of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is to accumulate reserves, but to serve the Canadian people and to try and grant as many loans as possible in order to promote the building of family housing units.
For instance, if I am not mistaken, the minister stated the other day that 100,000 dwelling units were needed in Canada. It is a truly extraordinary number of dwellings and when considering the needs of, families it is therefore urgent to take the means to facilitate the construction of housing units for all families who wish to take advantage of this legislation.
Mr. Chairman, I also note that the money will be drawn from the consolidated revenue fund, that is from taxes. I wish to point this out, because I consider that it is an extremely serious anomaly to tax Canadians once again in order to increase the assets of this corporation. In my opinion, owing to the power held by parliament, such a situation could easily be corrected by returning some regal rights the Bank of Canada. The latter could make some funds available to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at a nominal cost instead of levying them by means of taxes, as this bill seems ready to do.
That would make a truly substantial change and it would make capital directly available to the consumer, because it is said that activity in the building trade is a sign of prosperity. It is a fact that a great activity in the building trade is profitable to the whole nation.
On the other hand, when the building trade slows down, thousands of businesses are affected and thus, thousands of people are thrown out of work. Therefore, the federal government should take back its legal rights and grant the credit required to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at a nominal or administrative cost, because the system as it is actually advocated, is basically incorrect and fundamentally wrong.
[Mr. Cote (Chicoutimi) .1
Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that in the development of residential housing, it is important to consider that the majority of houses built today for families are a bit too small. Plans should be taken into consideration to provide for the building of larger houses to meet the requirements of families.
Another very important point is that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should not only grant loans in urban areas, but also in rural communities, because many family heads and individuals do not like to live in urban centres, but would like to build their own homes or have them built on contract. And if C.M.H.C. could grant them a loan, the social condition of a large number of families would be improved as a result.
Finally, I call the attention of the minister to the fact that the Quebec government grants a 3 per cent rebate on family houses in accordance with some rather strict standards. The federal government, in my opinion, should consider the possibility and feasibility of granting a rebate of at least 3 per cent to all the borrowers who took advantage of the National Housing Act because, as some hon. members mentioned, it is a difficult problem today for thousands of family heads to meet their monthly instalments, because the interest rate is too high.
Therefore, that advantage of a 3 per cent rebate should in fact be extended to all parts of Canada and not only to a special area of our country. It would a wonderful opportunity to be of assistance to the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to address a few words on this subject, as one who comes from a constituency which has within its limits not only one third of the existing public housing in Canada but also substantial areas of ground which should be redeveloped for public housing or otherwise included in an urban renewal program.
I should like to make a few comments on what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. He referred to the fact that in the city of Toronto we have been dilatory over the years in developing the south side of Queen street. He was critical, I gathered, because this project is not going forward. I would point out that the development proposed for the south side of Queen street is not a housing development but a commercial redevelopment. In my opinion housing has a priority which should be well ahead of the kind of civic monument which is in the minds of those who are contemplating this redevelopment.

One aspect of the speeches made by both the hon. member for Winnipeg North and the hon. member for Vancouver East was an exhortation to the minister to get on with this particular job. Both of them ignored the fact that responsibility for the primary initiative has under the constitution of our country been given to the municipalities. It is with the municipalities that the initiative in this field lies. It is they who must decide how the downtown areas are to be redeveloped, how land is to be used, and so on. It is they who must put up the basic equity which will make these developments possible.
However, I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North that there have been serious shortcomings from the municipal standpoint. He gave a number of examples from Winnipeg and I will give one from my own riding. In an area not a mile away from where Toronto is proudly raising its new city hall, down a narrow laneway with broken sidewalks can be found a row of 15 or more houses about 75 years old, leaning at a precarious angle, with windows broken and the refuse deposits of several weeks lying outside uncollected. My visit was made in January of this year in response to a request for assistance. In the house I entered there was no running water in the bathroom, the toilet had fallen off the wall on to the floor, the ceiling had fallen in in several rooms and in one, immediately above the kitchen, it was possible to see right through the floor. The furnace was not operating and had not been operating since October. I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that my visit was in January and that the city of Toronto has a specific bylaw requiring landlords in these circumstances to heat buildings. I was advised subsequently by the public health inspector for Toronto that he had had to issue an order requiring the tenants to clean out the lice and cockroaches in this building. Yet for this hovel the occupants were paying $55 a month, a substantial amount of what they were receiving from city welfare sources. Once again, this is not something out of Oliver Twist in 19 th century Britain, nor is it mid-depression Britain pictured by George Orwell in "The Road to Wigan Pier". These are conditions which exist in metropolitan Toronto in 1964; I may have mentioned an extreme example, but many other such cases exist.
The root of the problem is failure on the part of the general public to realize that there are these pockets of bad living conditions and it is our responsibility and that of the public generally to recognize that they do exist. It rests with the municipalities to assume their responsibility in this connection. First of all, something must be done at the municipal level to enforce the bylaws already on the
National Housing Act
books. I brought the particular example I have just given to the attention of several municipal councillors in Toronto and they looked with horror on my suggestion that the bylaws should be enforced, pointing out that the enforcement of bylaws was unpopular politically. I am not suggesting that this problem will be solved by mass housing developments of the kind which have been referred to by one or two hon. members. In 1949, with assistance from the federal government, the Regent Park North project was built in Toronto largely at the instance of the late Mayor Robert Saunders. This was followed in 1956 and 1957 by the Regent Park South project, the two together making up about 3,500 units. These particular projects, which led to the congregation of a large number of residents in a relatively small area, engendered social problems all their own. It is reassuring to note from the resolution on the order paper that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has learned from the Regent Park experience that it is far better to partially dehabilitate an area, using some of the existing structures where possible, as opposed to the mass levelling and reconstruction which was carried out in the case of Regent Park. In the case of Regent Park South, the land cost over half a million dollars an acre. With the adoption of the policy set out in this resolution, more and more adequate housing can be achieved for low income families with the same expenditure of the tax dollar. Equally, by retaining some of the houses in private ownership and by selective redevelopment we can also avoid the segregation of many welfare cases into a small area, which has inclined to create its own type of social problem in some of our developments.
I would also like to bring to the attention of the minister some further requirements which in the future I would like to see added to the National Housing Act. First I would like to see provision made in the National Housing Act to provide mass developments such as Regent Park South, and area redevelopments with recreation centres and facilities for children so that some of the social problems which have arisen in mass housing projects in which there are insufficient recreation facilities can be overcome.
I would also echo the sentiments of the hon. member for Greenwood earlier this day, when he pointed to the work of one of the vice presidents of my association, Mrs. May Birchard, toward providing daytime shelters for out of work and unemployable men. I would like to see in time a resolution introduced into this house to amend the statute to make it possible, in those areas where residential redevelopment is not possible, to

National Housing Act
clear the land and then have the city sell or lease it on a long term basis for commercial or industrial purposes in order to improve the economics of housing development elsewhere in the city. Perhaps our cities could be assisted in this way. In the example I have mentioned the project is within a quarter of a mile of major rail lines and of the new Gardiner expressway. Very obviously land is of great value there for commercial or industrial purposes. It should be possible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to assist in the development of that land for commercial purposes and then to use the profit gained to subsidize improved housing development elsewhere in the city. We have heard a great deal in the last year or so about Michael Harrington's "hidden poor", that group which in one way or another our existing social measures fail to reach. Better housing will not answer all the problems of the hidden poor, but without providing better living accommodation for them none of the other social measures we might have can hope to be successful. I therefore hope that this resolution will soon pass and C.M.H.C. will be empowered by the provisions included in the resolution, to support the municipalities in engaging in this type of urban renewal project.
