Mr. Chairman, it was not our
intention to hold up this resolution at all at this stage. No member of this party has risen this evening, in the hope that the committee would pass the measure through the resolution stage and we would have the bill before us. The minister informed me in a discussion I had with him that the bill has been printed and is now ready for distribution, and we have been hoping all day that the resolution would pass and we could have the bill before us so we could offer some substantive contribution to the specific measures to be enacted. Now, since several members of the parties to my left, and a government member have entered the debate I think it is only fair, even though in all likelihood there will be no acknowledgement of the co-operation we are endeavouring to give the government in this matter, to say a few words on this subject. None the less, we are eager to see the resolution stage dispensed with, and I would submit to all members of the house through you, Mr. Chairman, that more constructive contributions can be made to the debate once the bill is before us and once we have the specific proposals before the committee, particularly as they concern problems in connection with the operation of the act in local constituencies.
I could say, Mr. Chairman, that the last government, the Progressive Conservative government, when it was in office did more in that short time to improve the operation of

the National Housing Act than any other government since the act was first introduced in 1935. But I will not say that because I do not want to take up the time of the house in doing so. I could, too, say that the provisions of the resolution the committee has before it are substantially the provisions of the measures that were proposed by the former government or an extension of those measures that were brought in by the former government. But I will not take up the time of the house in doing that tonight either; I think it is important that the resolution stage be proceeded with and dispensed with so we can have the bill before us.
On behalf of this party, the official opposition, I will say that we endorse those remarks that have already been made with respect to the late minister, Jack Garland, and Mr. Stewart Bates. I knew Mr. Bates personally and I received nothing but cooperation from him, and always a dedication to the operation of the act for the benefit of all Canadians. Suffice it to say that the resolution itself substantially contains provisions which were proposed by the former government, with one or two exceptions, the loans to existing homes, and so on. These are very good provisions and ones which would have seen the light of day had we not been faced with the obstructionism of the then opposition whose members now sit on the government benches.
The minister has made reference to the Winnipeg urban renewal scheme. This is a project to which he attached great importance as one of the largest in Canadian housing history. We, of course, are bound to agree with him. Here again, the Winnipeg scheme was conceived, generated and commenced by the previous government and we have nothing but praise for that scheme. I am sure the minister wants to be fair and will immediately concede that this is so. Also the provisions with regard to the extension of loans for the construction of accommodation for university students was another measure with which the former government was concerned. So I could go on, Mr. Chairman, but I do not want to take up the time of the committee in going through them item by item.
However, there are one or two provisions in the resolution which are of interest and we will have to wait until we see the bill before we can be constructive in our contributions with respect to these matters. I would hope, once again, that we can get the resolution through this evening and have the bill before us. It has been printed and is ready for distribution. Once we have it before us I am sure we will all be in a much better position to make some constructive contribution to the debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks about this resolution. After looking through the different items in it, it is my belief that we should be attempting to give more aid to municipalities, especially those municipalities with large national housing projects and those considering urban development. I would like to speak for a few minutes this evening on the question of land assembly or the federal-provincial development which we have in Peterborough. This development was set up in 1952 by the federal government, the provincial government and the municipality of Peterborough. It includes 660 acres and the intention was to have a continuous supply of lots, but from 1952 to 1957 there was very little accomplished with regard to this development. Since 1957 a total of 692 lots have been developed and built on; but this has been accomplished over a period of 12 years, with most of the development taking place after 1957.
This is one of the largest developments in Canada at the present time. This development was divided into four or five phases but it has not given contractors and individuals a steady supply of serviced lots. I do not know whether this fault lies with the federal government, the provincial government or the municipality. This type of planning when there are no serviced lots for contractors or individuals to purchase is not good for the city. I should like to point out to the minister that this is the type of development that hinders any private developer competing in such a project. This is where I feel the federal government should consider more assistance to municipalities if this type of development is to continue.
I should like to read part of the agreement which the federal and provincial governments have signed with the city of Peterborough, and I imagine other municipalities have also signed similar agreements. This is what is required by the city in regard to services:
At its own expense, to provide all trunk services which may be required to the edge of the project.
This item alone I feel adds a considerable burden to any municipality's tax structure. These services entail main trunk sewers, water mains and storm drains. I would also mention that traffic arteries must be built to service large land assembly projects.
Another item to which I should like to refer asks the city that no municipal tax rate or charges of any nature whatsoever be levied by the city while the lots are owned by or on behalf of the corporation. In 1952 the city turned over to the corporation 660 acres of land to develop. Since that time the city has received no taxes from this property unless it was developed and sold. This has been a
National Housing Act
subsidy that the city has been asked to carry. No private developer has ever had such concessions.
I consider that in the case of the city of Peterborough the city has lost thousands of dollars in taxes over the past 12 years. On checking with the municipality I understand that this land assembly at the present time which is owned by the corporation is assessed at $500,000. With a mill rate of 70 mills on the dollar, this amounts to $35,000 being lost by the city in taxes. Spread over 12 years means that close to $400,000 may be owed to the city of Peterborough by the corporation. I do not feel that these concessions should be granted the corporation.
Right now in this land assembly there are only ten lots available and there will be no more available this year. There are no services in there at the present time. When this site was chosen for the project I do not think consideration was given to the distance to the sewage plants. It has been an expensive drain to the city, which services the area with trunk sewers. The corporation is authorizing help for municipalities with sewage treatment plants. I think they should consider main trunk sewers, especially for this type of project. If the municipality is responsible for supplying these services it may be a reason why they are not advancing with these projects as fast as they should. The trunk service which went to this land assembly a few years ago cost over $1 million. I do not feel that all of this amount went into services in this area, but most of it did, and I understand that another trunk sewer service will be needed there shortly.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think the corporation should add to paragraph (g) of the resolution, along with sewage treatment projects, main trunk sewers, water mains and storm drains which will service housing projects. We must also consider main arteries for traffic with which municipalities such as mine find themselves saddled. For this reason I think the government should consider assistance for main streets or thoroughfares which are going to service this type of development.
In the agreement to which I referred there is also an item regarding the engineering of the project. The city is asked to carry out engineering designs of all services required by the project. Such engineering design is to include field investigation, surveying, preliminary and final planning and preparation of all plans, working drawings and specifications. After they are finished the city is allowed to pick up 3 per cent of the cost of this project from the corporation. Any businessman realizes that any engineering or

National Housing Act
consulting firm would get at least 10 per cent on this type of work. I imagine that this government would not want to pay anything less, and here again I feel that the cities are subsidizing the corporation.
Another feature I should like to bring out regarding this project, something which the contractors must contend with, is that when lots are being purchased in land assemblies the builders must pay double price. If the lot is selling for $1,500 to individuals a builder must pay $3,000; and on completion of the home, if the builder sells it at the price set by C.M.H.C. he is refunded the extra $1,500 which he paid for the lot. This is referred to as an end price. I realize that this clause was inserted to protect the public from speculators and builders, but at the present time I do not think that these controls are desirable or necessary. Competition among contractors building this type of home makes it very unlikely that prices will rise. It might also encourage builders to put better workmanship and materials into the homes if this selling price is not applied. This set price tends to make builders cut corners and thus lower the standard of the homes which people are purchasing today.
I have spoken to the minister regarding this matter and I feel that he is going to have an answer for me. I feel that the corporation should take a careful look at the Peterborough area and other similar areas with a View to seeing that more lots are made available for builders, so that cities such as Peterborough are not left to pick up all the cost of these subsidies. I understand that the federal and provincial governments lose no money in this type of development, but I feel the municipalities are certainly subsidizing them. I feel that if these subsidies are needed they should be carried out by the government. Before I sit down, I should like to say that I am not criticizing this development in Peterborough or this type of project. I am criticizing the financial burden that is being loaded upon the municipalities.

speechtext:
I want to say that I rise to support the resolution. Personally, I am very pleased to note the provisions relating to further assistance to provinces and municipalities in carrying out urban renewal programs authorized by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This is a very important aspect of this question to a number of communities in my constituency. I am very glad that the measure will provide for the inclusion of existing houses in urban renewal programs. Then there is the matter of providing loans to co-operative associations and charitable corporations to assist in the construction of accommodation for university students and their families. The resolution also refers to authorizing the corporation to make loans and contributions to provincially or municipally owned housing agencies for public housing projects or subsidized housing accommodation for families of low income. I believe that that is very necessary indeed.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks. I must say that I appreciated the tone and the tenor of the minister's remarks.
I thought his opening statement introducing this resolution was most appropriate. It is obvious some considerable thought has been given by the minister and the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the particular needs in Canada at this time which make these amendments necessary. I have a few suggestions to make. In contrast to the hon. member for Yukon, I do attempt to have ideas.
First of all, I suggest to the minister that greater consideration should be given to the smaller communities, especially in the unorganized districts. I am not underestimating what corporation officials have tried to do in the past. The insurance companies have overlooked these isolated villages, incorporated or unincorporated, because I understand they do not like the cost of administration from a central office in Vancouver, or some large city. There is also the difficulty that ensues as a result of their distance from the investment and the lack of opportunity to oversee it periodically. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has the staff and the facilities to render these services and to give advice to the organizations and people in

these smaller communities who are anxious to take advantage of the provisions of the act and who will be more anxious to take advantage of the amendments that are indicated now.
I make this suggestion, Mr. Chairman, to the minister that there should be more visits by officials of the corporation to the smaller communities. I realize that this is not always easy, but they should contact the proper organizations which, in some cases, will be the city council, the chamber of commerce, the Rotary club, the Legion, farmers' and women's institutes or other organizations. The corporation officials should advise them as to what can be done under the act, and the policy of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with regard to the administration of the regulations relating to the various sections of the act.
Now, I believe it is necessary that there be a wider understanding of the purposes of the act and of the opportunities that are provided under the act. If I may give an illustration, last year one or two communities in my constituency were quite put out about the fact that organizations and individuals could not obtain loans from the corporation in areas that were outside the accepted or, shall I say, the ancient boundaries of the village. I discussed this with one of the senior officials. I forget his name, but he was the least bureaucratic type of person I have ever met. He came up to my office and explained the whole situation. I asked him to write me a letter outlining the policy of the corporation in this respect. Then I was able to send this letter back to the organizations concerned and to the builders concerned. They were quite satisfied because they realized they were not being picked on. They were under the impression at the time that this little community was the subject of some discrimination. Once they understood the situation, the feeling of indignation passed away. There has been a local official visit this district and give a talk to the chamber of commerce, but he dealt with the situation on a purely local basis without indicating to them that this was a national policy and there was no discrimination.
I believe that there should be a great deal done to increase the understanding of the act and the advantage that can be taken of it. In this way, a good deal of misunderstanding would be avoided. I want to support what previous members have said in respect of the need for the extension of homes for senior citizens. In my opinion, it is pathetic to witness the distress of older people who are wrenched away from their friends and familiar surroundings because they have to go to a larger centre to live in one of these homes for senior citizens. I do urge that
National Housing Act
special consideration be given to this problem by the officials of the corporation. They should go to these smaller communities and inform interested local organizations such as chambers of commerce, women's and farmers' institutes, the Legion, Rotary clubs and so on, who may be interested in sponsoring one of these projects, what can be done under the act. Their advice in planning a project like that would be most useful indeed.
I have been asked to bring to the attention of the minister the need for increased accommodation in the city of Nelson. I am not going to speak at length; I am going to give him the details of these complaints later. I have been asked to mention this in the house-

speechtext:
I am watching the clock. I said I was not going to detain the passage of the resolution. However, when I have been asked by my constituents to rise in this house and speak, I do so, and nobody stops me.
In any event, I have been asked to raise the question and I want to deal very briefly with the correspondence. I have a letter here from the editor of the Nelson Daily News, who is very concerned about this situation that exists in Nelson.
He says:
A private concern by the name of Transco Development Limited has indicated their intention and desire to construct a large high rise apartment building in Nelson with accommodation for slightly over 70 families. Financing is being attempted through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
There seems to exist in the minds of C.M. and H. officials some doubt as to the need for decent accommodations in the city of Nelson to the extent proposed. From my own personal experience in Nelson I can truthfully state that there is a decided lack of decent rental accommodation in Nelson from the standpoint of housing or apartments. Most of the available rental facilities are of ancient construction and many of them stand vacant for this very reason. Many people are unwilling to accept substandard accommodation and poor living conditions when their income would provide much better if only the proper type of facilities were available.
It would be a shame if the city of Nelson were to lose this opportunity to provide a mere handful of families a decent place in which to live. As member for Kootenay West you can do your constituents a great service by bringing this matter to the attention of the proper authorities in Ottawa and perhaps it would be a good idea if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was informed that the people of the Kootenays will not sit still much longer waiting for development and progress which only easier financing can attract. Perhaps it is time that people of the Kootenay investigated the possibility of bringing

National Housing Act
American development funds into the province. I trust that you will give this matter your early attention, sir.
Then I have a letter from the corporation of the city of Nelson in somewhat similar vein. I have another letter from Nelson school district No. 7 about a survey. I have another letter from the Nelson chamber of commerce in similar vein. I also have numerous letters from various firms in Nelson interested in the building of these apartments and quite a large number of letters from persons employed in Nelson who are seeking accommodation. I urge the minister and his officials to give further consideration to the need for increased accommodation in Nelson to meet the increase in employment, population and economic activity.
I have one other matter to mention and I am quite sure that if the hon. member for Port Arthur was here he would say that this is a Victorian idea. I am accused by my colleagues on some occasions of having some Victorian ideas. I have raised this question before but I have not had a very sympathetic response from any former minister or the officials. However, I expect a more sympathetic response from the present minister because he knows something about the lumber industry. He has been closely associated with it and he knows all about forest materials.
I suggest that when houses are being built in a district where lumbering is the major industrial activity, every consideration should be given to using wood in its various forms in the building of houses, instead of shipping in asbestos shingles. If they are put on the side of a house and a boy happens to throw a rock at them they break up in a year or two. I urge that every consideration be given to permitting the building of houses from local materials as far as possible, and in our district of course they are wood products.
My second suggestion is that consideration should be given to loans to persons who wish to build log homes. This is a point about which I can well understand the hon. member for Port Arthur might snort, but I think the suggestion offers some scope for the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to investigate. In the Kootenays we have young men who are building homes and are importing synthetic materials. They are putting asbestos roofs on their homes. At the same time Californians are coming up to the Kootenays and taking pictures of the exterior and interior of log homes. Then they are going back to California and buying logs, and these very men who are buying asbestos for the roofs of their houses are making shakes to be sent to California at a terrific price.
I happen to be one of those persons who are interested in the production of shakes,
[Mr. Herridge.l
and if the minister or his officials will read the literature with respect to the value of shakes they will realize that they make the most efficient roof that has been devised by mankind to date. I have shakes on the roof of my office which were put there in 1898, and they are almost as good today as the day they were put on.
I do ask that consideration be given to the granting of loans to persons who can prove that they can have nice log homes built. We have plenty of first class timber of the right type. We have plenty of cedar for the production of shakes. I should like to see some variety in homes. I am not suggesting that this type of home would be suitable in the suburbs of a large city, but this type of home is very suitable in small communities and rural areas. I do urge that consideration be given to introducing some variety into housing designs. I am one who is not much given to conformity. I should not like to live in a house that was exactly the same as my neighbour's, and like hundreds of others in the same suburb. I like variety, and I think most people do if they get the opportunity to take advantage of it. I do urge that consideration be given to the granting of loans to persons who want to build log homes.
We have a lot of young men in our district who are quite capable axmen. They are interested in it, and once they see log homes and see the possibilities for beauty both on the exterior and the interior they are very taken with them. They would like the opportunity to use their own skills and local materials in order to build homes that would be most suited to the district in which they would be built, and would be something a little different from the uniform houses that are produced today, and I suppose necessarily so because of the attempt to reduce costs. I see that you are looking at me with a rather anxious eye, Mr. Chairman, so at this point I will conclude my remarks.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Nicholson thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-102, to amend the National Housing Act, 1954.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: SUGGESTION FOR ONE
SUGGESTION FOR ONE
subsubtopic: DISTINCTIVE DESIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 6 last I asked the following question of the Prime Minister:
In view of the fact that Canada has been an adult and independent country since the Statute of Westminster, could the Prime Minister assure the house that his government will give us but one distinctive national flag, without union jack or red ensign, so that Canada may not be mistaken for some foreign country as happened at the time of the Suez crisis?
Mr. Speaker, personally I object entirely to the inclusion of either the union jack or the red ensign in any bill for, in my opinion, both flags represent imperialism and foreign domination.
I would prefer a bill establishing a single distinctive flag bearing, for instance, a single maple leaf.
Those who are against the inclusion of such a symbol because there are no maple
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion trees in certain parts of the country should remember that the coat of arms of Canada includes lions and yet, I have never seen one in our forests.
The government is asking us to take illogical action when it invites us to accept two flags.
Mr. Speaker, what would you think of Napoleon if, when he was crowned emperor of the French, he had proclaimed the tricolour as the official flag of France to please the revolutionists and if, at the same time, he had kept the white flag fleur-de-lis to keep the support of the Bourbons and the aristocrats?
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Minister of Justice will have another try at it, for he failed in his duty by accepting two flags, including the union jack; I hope he will make amends, so that we may have one distinctive flag which will be a symbol of unity and not a symbol of division in the country.
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of only one flag, without any foreign symbol, because we are a sovereign nation which, on the domestic level, is self-governing and, on the international level, is not subservient to any other country.
Sovereign does not mean absolute, for every country is subject to public international law.
We can state with pride that our country enjoys today the eight main attributes of a sovereign state.
These are the right to legislate; the right to give our legislation extraterritoriality; the right to have diplomatic representation abroad; the right to have Canadian courts of last appeal; the right to declare peace, war or neutrality; the right to amend our constitution according to our wish and our decision; the right to negotiate and sign our own treaties; and finally, the recognition of our sovereignty by the other countries of the world.
Many factors and events have enabled the realization of such a maturity. But the most outstanding was the Statute of Westminster passed on December 11. 1931-
Mr. Speaker, I took my inspiration for the foregoing from a speech made in the house a few years ago by the former member for Sherbrooke, Mr. Maurice Allard.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the government will reconsider the matter and make amends.
We have seen tonight on parliament hill a scene of division which reflects to some extent the picture of our country today.
I hope that the government will give us only one distinctive national flag and not two. Personally, I would rather see it wait a few years instead of giving us two symbols, two flags representing two Canadas, that is the complete destruction of national unity.

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- WITHDRAWAL OF FILM RESPECTING PRIME MINISTER
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- WITHDRAWAL OF FILM RESPECTING PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Since I raised this question in the house I had an opportunity to make remarks about it the other night in the grievance period, but there was no answer from the government benches. I intend to put the question again with some added information. I see the Prime Minister's valuable, emotional and colourful parliamentary secretary is here and I am looking forward to a brilliant response to my question, such as he gave last week when he entertained us all with that wonderful reading from one of the Prime Minister's speeches.
The question; is really the relationship between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Prime Minister's office, an independent producer of films, Intervideo Productions Limited and its head, Richard Ballentine. I should like to begin by putting on record some opinions of one George Hogan which appear tonight in the Toronto Telegram because in this case I agree with the opinions expressed and I think they set out the points I wish to make. Mr. Hogan says:
The C.B.C. has the right not to show the film if it so wishes. And I personally think the country's Prime Minister ought to have the right to ask that a film about himself not be shown if he feels it will be personally or politically harmful.
But surely neither has the right to achieve these purposes by hiding behind charges which may well destroy the career of a man who has done his job in good faith.
That seems to be the problem. The latest news in this case is that the C.B.C. has informed Mr. Ballentine that it refuses to pay him for the services rendered in connection with this film unless he gives up the slash prints which he feels he will have to show in order to vindicate his reputation. Well, I am making an effort in association with some other members to arrange for the railway committee room to be available some night so that Mr. Ballentine can show the film there and be sure of an audience of people who will perhaps be most expert in judging

whether the film is good or not. We shall put it on and see what led Mr. Reeves Hagan of the C.B.C. to say that it was just a peep show and that the production showed a lack of intellectual grasp.
I have been trying to find out something about the Prime Minister's lack of intellectual grasp, or his intellectual grasp, by reading some of his material and I have not yet arrived at any decision because it is a hard thing to decide whether a person lacks intellectual grasp or not. I want to begin this part of my comment by saying, though, that the Prime Minister obviously is not very decisive if he has to bring in every Tom, Dick and Mary to give an opinion as to whether this is a good film and puts him in a good light or not. I think one of the real unfortunate aspects of this is that though we have a minister of culture, the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), he was not even called in to look at the film. Instead, we have Tom Kent saying it is brilliant, Mitchell Sharp saying it is an astounding document and Keith Davey telling us it is absolutely brilliant. And still it was turned down.
I want to ask whether it was turned down because it showed the Prime Minister trying to make a difficult decision about whether he wanted to watch the world series game or hear from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) about the S.I.U. problem which was forcing itself forward into a crisis. This may seem picayune but it is important. Why, after six months preparation, after all these screenings, after all this enthusiasm by the C.B.C. and its public affairs department, was there this sudden switch? Either the Prime Minister, after all this advice from his coterie, who gave their decisions as to whether it would show him in a favourable light, so informed the C.B.C. and they switched, or we need an answer from the C.B.C. as to how they can be so wasteful and extravagant and so much off on the wrong track to spend six months and $35,000 on something that at the last minute they say is not technically good enough. The question arises whether Mr. Hagan, the public affairs representative who was dealing with this matter, was overruled by the senior people in the C.B.C. If they did overrule him, does it come down to the fact that the senior executives of the C.B.C. overrule the heads of their departments? Or did they get a message from the Prime Minister's office? We do not know. All we know is that this is one of the silliest, most wasteful affairs imaginable. On the one hand, they spent all this time and money to find out that something was technically inferior at the end, and so publicly slur the producer; or it is a really tragic situation of inadequate liaison between the Prime Minister's office and the C.B.C.

I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we have to have answers to these questions, and we need good, clear answers. Questions have been put on this subject and I think we should have a reply from the government now. Before concluding, I would like to say a word about this aspect of the matter. I hope we can prevail upon the government so that we can see this slash print that the C.B.C. demands back and which they want to suppress. I hope we can see it right here on parliament hill, so we can get the whole story on the world series and see whether its producer is so technically incompetent as the C.B.C. has had the nerve to say.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- WITHDRAWAL OF FILM RESPECTING PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to the film "Mr. Pearson-the man and the office", two things, I think, should be made quite clear: first, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation thought up the idea; and second, it was the C.B.C. which finally decided not to release the film. This was to be a candid camera production; it was to cover a day in the life of a Canadian prime minister; it was to cover private discussions with cabinet ministers; it was to show policy being formed. As some of this material was bound to be confidential, and because the dignity of the office of the prime minister had to be protected, the Prime Minister asked for the right to review the film. The right was readily granted and work began.
During the editing stage the film was viewed on four separate occasions. On two occasions the Prime Minister himself was present; the first was in December in Toronto, to see the earliest assembled version, and the second was in Ottawa after substantial editing but without the advantage of a sound track. All discussions as to content were carried on with the C.B.C. by members of the Prime Minister's staff, principally Mr. O'Hagan. Every effort was made to protect the editorial prerogatives of the producer.
The office of the Prime Minister is content that there was no transgression in this area. At no time was any judgment as to the quality of the film transmitted to the C.B.C., formally or informally, by any member of the government or any representative of the Prime Minister.

subtopic: ALASKA HIGHWAY
ALASKA HIGHWAY
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question that stands in my name concerns the Alaska highway, and I am glad to see that of all the responsible ministers who were supposed to be here tonight to answer questions, the Minister of Northern Affairs and 20220-243
1, 1964	3829
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion National Resources (Mr. Laing) is at least in his seat. The question arises out of a press report I read in the Montreal Gazette concerning a speech the minister made in Vancouver to the Vancouver chamber of commerce. The Gazette refers to the minister as having at last caught the vision, which they term the bold, booming vision. The contents of his remarks to the chamber in Vancouver inferred, according to the press article at least, that there had been some discussion with the government of the United States with respect to a joint cost-sharing project for the paving of the Alaska highway. The minister knows that I have asked several questions on this subject in this house over the last year of the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Public Works, and of the minister himself.
I should like to read to him now a copy of a letter which I have in my possession written by Mr. Frederick G. Dutton, the assistant secretary to Mr. Rusk of the United States. The letter is headed up on department of state stationery of the United States government and is addressed to congressman Rivers, with whom I have co-operated for some time in regard to the paving of the Alaska highway. The letter is dated March 11, 1964, and reads as follows:
Dear Congressman Rivers:
I refer to my letter to you of November 15, 1963 in response to yours of November 5 requesting that this department open discussions with the government of Canada to ascertain whether or not Canada is sufficiently interested in the idea of blacktopping the Alaska highway to consider some joint cost sharing arrangements.
As I said in my previous letter, the department felt it necessary to review the matter with other interested agencies prior to opening any discussions with the Canadian government. In the absence of a United States government initiative in support of such a proposal, the department 'did not feel that a direct approach to the Canadian government requesting their views was appropriate. However, the department has taken the opportunity of calling to the attention of the Canadian government the bills recently introduced into congress, H.R. 9667 and H.R. 9716, and S. 2417, relating to this proposal and providing copies for its information.
The minister is also aware that last February 21, 1964 I asked a question in this regard of the Minister of Public Works, and his reply indicated that until an economic assessment had been completed on the economic feasibility of paving the Alaska highway the Canadian government did not intend to proceed further with it.
My specific question last Friday, I believe it was, to the minister asked for his comments with respect to the press article, and whether the Canadian government had had any discussions with the United States government, formal or informal, which would justify the minister stipulating in Vancouver
3830	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that if the United States government offered to pay the whole cost of the paving of the highway the Canadian government should accept such a proposal. That is the way the press printed the story. It may have been distortion, because apparently several ministers have been complaining about being given unfair press treatment of late, and perhaps the minister of northern affairs did not say that in Vancouver. However, I am sure that I and certainly the house would be interested in this matter.
I am also wondering whether the minister would tell us whether or not any negotiations are now under way, formal or otherwise, with the government of the United States or any agency of the United States government with respect to any paving program on the Alaska highway; whether it is to be a joint cost sharing program or whether it is to be paid for in whole by the United States; or whether the Canadian government intends to pave the highway on its own.
The other question I am interested in and I am sure the house is interested in is this. If such discussions have not yet taken place, when does the minister anticipate they might take place? The minister seems to have had this information at his fingertips when he addressed the Vancouver chamber of commerce, and my constituents in the Yukon are very vitally interested in this highway, since it contributes substantially, as the minister well knows, to the economic well-being of the Yukon throughout the length of the highway in the Yukon. Since the army will be moving out almost entirely by the end of this month, with the Department of Public Works taking over the maintenance operation-I am sure they will do an excellent job-there is a reduction of approximately $1,200,000 a year in the army payroll in the Whitehorse area alone. Therefore we are all extremely interested in what are the plans for the paving of the highway, and I would suggest that the minister take this opportunity of giving some information to the people of the Yukon regarding the government's plans for the paving of the Alaska highway. Since the minister has made certain statements to the Vancouver chamber of commerce, I think this is the least the people of the Yukon are entitled to from the minister this evening.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ALASKA HIGHWAY
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am quite certain that there is no subject of greater interest to the people in western Canada, nor one of any greater economic interest to the people of the whole of Canada, than having a modern Alaska highway. This high-

way was built in 1944 as a war measure by the United States at an estimated cost at that time of $125 million. In 1946 it was turned over to Canada without cost by the United States government. Since that time it has been improved on the southern end, from mile zero at Dawson Creek, by about 83J miles of paving northward. I am very proud to be able to say that the paving was done by a government represented by this side of the house and not the other.
If my hon. friend from Yukon is somewhat jealous and envious of the further activity we have undertaken in respect of the Alaska highway, I can understand that. We have been extremely energetic to see to it that we can amass public opinion, not only in British Columbia, in Alberta and in the prairie provinces, but particularly in the western tier of the United States which, as the hon. member will realize, notably Montana, would profit most from the use of this highway. We happen to be the corridor through which access by land is necessary if two parts of the United States are going to be put together. It seems to me that as a good friend and neighbour of the United States we owe it to them to provide better accommodation for a land connection as equitably as we possibly can. At the same time, I believe we owe ourselves the responsibility of seeing to it that we exploit the advantage we have as far as we possibly can.

speechtext: I am coming to that, if I have time. We have been in negotiation. First of all, the Department of Public Works embarked upon a cost review. They are working on that at the present time. Lately there has been an indication from the United States that they believe that tourism is the future of Alaska. It is quite obvious in discussions that took place here in Ottawa not very long ago with Mr. Udall, that the United States is desirous of making this a comfortable highway for traffic to Alaska. Negotiations through my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), have been begun through the ambassador who is at a comparable level in Washington, to get some idea of their idea of cost sharing. In the meantime we are embarking upon a cost benefit analysis which will be announced very shortly, parallel to the one undertaken by the Bat-telle institute.
